A railway brake helps slow down trains, control their speed going downhill, or keep them still when parked. It works similarly to brakes on cars, but is more complex because it needs to manage multiple connected carriages and still be effective without an engine. Clasp brakes are a type of brakes used on trains in the past.

M*A*S*H is an American story with many parts, including books, a movie, and TV shows. It is owned by 20th Century Fox (now 20th Century Studios) and is based on Richard Hooker's stories. The story is about a group of characters who work at a pretend hospital called "4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital" during the Korean War. In the 1970 movie, Donald Sutherland played a main character named Hawkeye Pierce. Alan Alda played the same character in the TV show with the same name. Later shows focused on characters from the original series after the war ended. Most versions of the story are funny but also show the difficult parts of being a doctor in a war. During their free time, the staff made jokes and had small disagreements. The story ended with the show "Trapper John, M.D." in 1986. Many people still like the series, and the company has sold DVDs of the movie and TV seasons.

Extinction means the end of a type of living thing or a group of types, usually a species. The exact moment of extinction is often hard to know, usually determined after the species is gone. Sometimes, a species thought to be extinct suddenly appears again in old fossils. Most species, over five billion in total, are believed to have disappeared. Today, around 8.7 million species of plants and animals are known, with many more microorganisms like bacteria possibly existing. Species come into being and thrive when they can adapt to a niche, or role, in their environment. They become extinct when they can no longer survive due to changes or competition. The relationship between animals and their niches is well understood. Most species last about 10 million years before dying out. Some, called living fossils, have changed little for hundreds of millions of years. Mass extinctions, where many species disappear at once, are rare but local extinctions are common. Scientists are concerned about the high rate of extinctions recently. Many species that become extinct are never studied. Some scientists predict up to half of current species might vanish by 2100. A 2018 report found that losing 300 mammal species would take 5 to 7 million years to recover. The 2019 "Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services" from IPBES states that wild mammal biomass has dropped 82%, half of natural ecosystems have been lost, and one million species are at risk. About 25% of plant and animal species are threatened. In June 2019, over a million plant and animal species were at risk. At least 571 species have gone extinct since 1750, likely more. Natural habitats, like forests, are destroyed for human activities such as farming. A dagger symbol (†) next to a species name usually means it is extinct.

The Boston National Historical Park includes sites that tell the story of Boston's role in the American Revolution. It became a national park on October 1, 1974. Seven out of eight sites are connected by the Freedom Trail, a walking tour through downtown Boston. All eight sites are national historic landmarks. Five of these sites are not owned or run by the National Park Service. They work together through agreements. The National Park Service runs visitor centers in Faneuil Hall and the Charlestown Navy Yard.

Stuart Leonard Miller (December 26, 1927 – January 4, 2015), nicknamed the Butterfly Man, was a right-handed pitcher who played in Major League Baseball. He played for the St. Louis Cardinals, Philadelphia Phillies, New York and San Francisco Giants, Baltimore Orioles, and Atlanta Braves from 1952 to 1968. Miller had a 105–103 record and a 3.24 earned run average, with 1164 strikeouts and 154 saves in 704 games pitched (93 as a starter). Miller was an All-Star for the Giants in 1961. In 1962, his ERA was 4.12, with a 5-8 record and 19 saves. The Giants traded him to the Baltimore Orioles in 1962. In 1963, Miller had a great season, with a 2.24 ERA, leading the American League in games, games finished, and saves. He finished seventh in the MVP voting in 1965, with a 14-7 record, a 1.89 ERA, and 24 saves. On April 30, 1967, Miller and Steve Barber pitched a no-hitter for the Orioles against the Detroit Tigers, but they lost 2–1. Miller allowed a run after Barber, who had walked ten batters. In the 1967 All-Star Game, a strong wind caused Miller to almost make a mistake, but he didn't fall off the mound. Roger Maris and Al Kaline advanced to second and third, and Al Kaline scored on an error. In the 10th inning, Miller's teammates helped him, and he became the winning pitcher. On May 14, 1967, Miller gave up Mickey Mantle's 500th career home run.

Priscilla Renea Hamilton, born on September 14, 1988, is an American singer and songwriter. She is with Capitol Records. Her first album, "Jukebox," came out on December 1, 2009. She is well-known for writing or co-writing popular songs like "California King Bed" for Rihanna, "Worth It" for Fifth Harmony, and "A No No" for Mariah Carey.

Mildred Ella "Babe" Didrikson Zaharias (June 26, 1911 – September 27, 1956) was an American athlete. She was very good at golf, basketball, baseball, and track and field. At the 1932 Summer Olympics, she won two gold medals in track and field. Later, she became a professional golfer and won 10 major championships in the LPGA. Many people think she was one of the greatest athletes ever.

Jim Jeffries, born on February 14, 1977, is an American-Canadian comedian, actor, and writer. He made a TV show called "Legit" from 2013 to 2014. He also hosted a late-night show on Comedy Central called "The Jim Jeffries Show" from 2017 to 2019.

Gauri Lankesh, born on January 29, 1962, and died on September 5, 2017, was a journalist and activist from Bangalore, Karnataka, India. She worked as an editor for "Lankesh Patrike," a Kannada weekly started by her father, P. Lankesh. She also ran her own weekly newspaper called "Gauri Lankesh Patrike." Gauri was shot and killed outside her home in Rajarajeshwari Nagar on September 5, 2017. At the time of her death, she was known for criticizing right-wing Hindu extremism. She was given the Anna Politkovskaya Award for speaking against right-wing Hindu extremism, supporting women's rights, and opposing caste discrimination.

In the Aztec and Nahua creation myths, there were five worlds before the current one. The present world is called the "fifth sun." In these myths, four previous worlds and their people were created and then destroyed by powerful gods. The Aztecs believed they were the "people of the sun." Their job was to keep the sun in the sky by offering blood and hearts in war. Without these offerings, the sun might disappear, harming the universe.
The Bank of America Tower may refer to buildings that were previously called the Bank of America Tower.
Ouanne is a town in the Yonne department, which is in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté in central France. There is also a river called Ouanne. This river starts near the town and flows into the Loing.

Dimitar Ivanov Berbatov, born on January 30, 1981, is a former professional Bulgarian footballer. A striker, he was the captain of the Bulgaria national team from 2006 to 2010 and is the team's all-time leading goalscorer. He is considered one of the best Bulgarian players of all time. Born in Blagoevgrad, Berbatov started his career with his hometown club Pirin before joining CSKA Sofia when he was 17 in 1998. In January 2001, he joined Bayer Leverkusen in Germany and played in his first Champions League final 18 months later, coming on as a substitute in the 2002 UEFA Champions League final, which Leverkusen lost to Real Madrid. After five-and-a-half years with Leverkusen, he moved to English club Tottenham Hotspur in July 2006 and stayed there for two years before joining Manchester United. He played in his second Champions League final in 2009, when his team lost 2–0 against Barcelona. During his time at Manchester United, which lasted four seasons, he won two Premier League titles in 2008–09 and 2010–11 and the Premier League Golden Boot in 2010–11. He then joined Fulham in August 2012 and later played for Monaco in France, PAOK in Greece, and Kerala Blasters in India before retiring at the end of the 2017-18 season. Berbatov made his debut for Bulgaria on November 17, 1999, at the age of 18. He represented Bulgaria in Euro 2004, which was the only major tournament he played in for his country. He became the team captain from 2006 to May 2010, when he retired from international football, ending his career with 48 goals from 78 matches. He also won the Bulgarian Footballer of the Year award seven times, breaking the record previously held by Hristo Stoichkov.

The saying "the road to hell is paved with good intentions" means that even good plans can lead to bad results. An alternative way to say this is "hell is full of good ideas, but heaven is full of good actions."
Eclectic is a town in Elmore County, Alabama, United States. It became a town in 1907. In 2010, it had 1,001 people living there. It is in the Montgomery metropolitan area.
Water Stratford is a village and civil parish. It is near the River Great Ouse in Aylesbury Vale, Buckinghamshire, England. It is west of Buckingham and close to the border with Oxfordshire.

Graduation is the giving of a diploma or degree to students. It can also be a special ceremony. The day of graduation is called graduation day. The ceremony itself is sometimes called commencement, convocation, or invocation.
Love Street" is a song by the American rock band The Doors. It is from their 1968 album called "Waiting for the Sun.

This article lists NHL teams' post-season appearances, Stanley Cup finals wins, Stanley Cup droughts, and other important details up to the 2019 Stanley Cup playoffs. Teams that have never made it to the post-season are noted by their first season in the league. Note: The 2004-05 season is not included. Of the current 31 NHL teams, 11 have never won the Stanley Cup. The Toronto Maple Leafs have had the longest Stanley Cup drought, which includes the entire expansion era, 52 seasons. Four teams have never reached the Stanley Cup finals: the Winnipeg Jets/Aztec Coyotes, Toronto Maple Leafs, Buffalo Sabres, and Florida Panthers. The longest Stanley Cup championship drought in history was 53 seasons for the New York Rangers, broken in 1994. The Toronto Maple Leafs currently have the longest active Stanley Cup drought at 52 seasons. In 2010, the Chicago Blackhawks ended their 47-season drought, the second-longest. From 2010 to 2012, three teams ended their long droughts: the Chicago Blackhawks, Boston Bruins, and Los Angeles Kings. The Florida Panthers have the longest active playoff series win drought, 23 seasons. The Winnipeg Jets/Aztec Coyotes broke their longest playoff series win drought in 2012 after 25 seasons. The Buffalo Sabres have the longest active playoff appearance drought, 9 seasons. The longest playoff droughts in history were 10 seasons for the Florida Panthers and Edmonton Oilers, which ended in 2012 and 2017, respectively.

Uranium-235 is an isotope of uranium found in about 0.72% of natural uranium. Unlike the more common isotope, uranium-238, uranium-235 can sustain a chain reaction. It is the only naturally occurring fissile isotope. Uranium-235 has a very long half-life of 703.8 million years. It was discovered in 1935 by Arthur Jeffrey Dempster. It can absorb slow neutrons and split into smaller parts, with a cross section of about 584.3±1 barns for slow neutrons. For fast neutrons, this is around 1 barn. Not all neutron absorptions lead to fission; some result in the formation of uranium-236.

Rūsiņš Mārtiņš Freivalds was a Latvian computer scientist and mathematician born on November 10, 1942, in Cēsuve. He became a member of the Latvian Academy of Sciences in 1992. Freivalds discovered an algorithm called Freivalds' algorithm, which checks if matrix products are correct. He taught at the University of Latvia, where students included Daina Taimiņa and Andris Ambainis. Freivalds passed away from a heart attack in Riga on January 4, 2016, at the age of 73.
Hera Hilmarsdóttir, known as Hera Hilmar, was born on December 27, 1988. She is an Icelandic actress. She began acting as a child in the 1990s. She started acting again in 2008.

A foundation, also known as a charitable foundation, is a type of nonprofit organization or charitable trust. It usually gives money and support to other charities through grants. However, it can also do charitable work directly. There are two main kinds of foundations: public charitable foundations, like community foundations, and private foundations, which are often funded by an individual or a family. Sometimes, the term "foundation" is used by organizations that don't give grants to the public.

A nucleosome is the basic building block for organizing DNA in eukaryotes. It consists of DNA wrapped around eight proteins called histones. Each nucleosome has a little less than two turns of DNA and includes two copies each of histone proteins H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. DNA needs to be packed into nucleosomes to fit inside the cell nucleus. In addition to nucleosomes, chromatin is further compacted into larger structures, eventually forming a chromosome. Nucleosomes carry information in the form of chemical changes on their histones. The position of nucleosomes in the DNA is important because it affects how accessible the DNA is to proteins that regulate genes. Nucleosomes were first seen in 1974 by Don and Ada Olins, and their structure, with about 200 DNA base pairs wrapped around histone proteins, was proposed by Roger Kornberg. The role of nucleosomes as gene regulators was shown by Lorch and others in experiments in 1987 and 1988. A nucleosome core includes about 146 DNA base pairs wrapped around a histone octamer. Linker DNA, up to 80 base pairs long, connects these cores. Technically, a nucleosome includes a linker region, but it is often used to mean just the core. Maps showing where nucleosomes are located in the genome are available for many organisms, like mouse liver and brain. Linker histones, such as H1, help pack DNA more tightly. Without linker histones, nucleosomes look like "beads on a string" under a microscope. In sperm cells, DNA is packed differently using proteins called protamines to make space for more DNA. Some archaea, like certain bacteria, also use nucleosomes, suggesting that using nucleosomes might not be unique to eukaryotes.

A gauleiter was the leader of a local Nazi party branch. This position was also the head of a "gau" or "reichsgau." The word can be used as singular or plural, depending on the context. Gauleiter was a Nazi party rank, the second highest, right below "Reichsleiter" and "Führer." During World War II, someone could become a gauleiter only if Adolf Hitler appointed them directly.

Raziya al-Din, also known as Razia Sultana, ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240. She was the first female Muslim ruler in the Indian subcontinent. She was the daughter of Sultan Shamsuddin Iltutmish. When her father was away in 1231-1232, she helped run the city. Iltutmish might have chosen her to be his heir. Instead, he was succeeded by Razia's half-brother, Ruknuddin Firuz, whose mother planned to harm Razia. During a rebellion against Ruknuddin, Razia got people to fight against her half-brother's mother. She became the ruler in 1236 after her half-brother was removed. Some nobles challenged Razia's rule, but she took more power over time. Her choice of non-Turkic officers made some nobles angry. In April 1240, she was removed from power after ruling for less than 4 years. She married one of the rebels, Ikhtiyaruddin Altunia, and tried to get back her throne but lost to her half-brother Muizuddin Bahram in October. She was killed shortly after.
Deer Park is a city in Hamilton County, Ohio, United States. It is near Cincinnati. According to the 2010 census, the population was 5,736.

Jordan's under-23 football team plays in international competitions like the Olympics and Asian Games. It also competes in other under-23, under-22, and under-21 tournaments. The team is managed by the Jordan Football Association. In 2013, Jordan's Olympic team won a bronze medal in the AFC U-22 Championship in Oman.

Ganesh Chaturthi, also known as Vinayaka Chavithi, is a Hindu festival celebrating Ganesh coming to Earth from Kailash Parvat with his mother, Goddess Parvati/Gauri. People set up Ganesh statues made of clay at home or in public spaces called pandals. Activities include chanting, prayers, and fasting. Sweet offerings like modaka are given and shared with the community. The festival lasts ten days. On the last day, the statues are immersed in water with music and singing. In Mumbai, about 150,000 statues are immersed each year. Afterward, the clay dissolves and Ganesh is believed to return to Kailash. The festival honors Ganesh as the god of new beginnings, remover of obstacles, wisdom, and intelligence. It is celebrated widely in India, particularly in Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Telangana, Odisha, West Bengal, Gujarat, and Chhattisgarh. In Tamil Nadu, it is usually celebrated at home. The festival is also observed in Nepal and by the Hindu diaspora in countries like Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Malaysia, Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana, Suriname, the Caribbean, Fiji, Mauritius, South Africa, the United States, and Europe. There, readings of texts and group feasting happen, along with athletic and martial arts competitions.

Indiana University of Pennsylvania (IUP) is a public research university in Indiana County, Pennsylvania. In fall 2019, it had 8,279 undergraduate students and 2,079 postgraduate students, making a total of 10,348 students. The university is located northeast of Pittsburgh. It is run by a local council of trustees and the board of governors of the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education. IUP also has branch campuses in Punxsutawney, Northpointe, and Monroeville. The university is accredited by the Middle States Commission on Higher Education.
Vacallo is a town in the Mendrisio district of Ticino in Switzerland. It is the first or last village in Valle di Muggio.

The 2006 Winter Paralympic Games, also called the IX Giochi Paralimpici Invernali in Italian, were the ninth Winter Paralympics. They happened in Turin, Italy, from March 10 to 19, 2006. These were the first Winter Paralympic Games in Italy. They were also the first Paralympics to use a new logo.
McIntire is a city in Mitchell County, Iowa, in the United States. In 2010, the population was 122.

Ronald Vaughan Joyce, born on October 19, 1930, and passed away on January 31, 2019, was a Canadian entrepreneur and billionaire. He co-founded Tim Hortons, a doughnut chain, in 1964 with Tim Horton, who was his partner and first franchisee. After Tim Horton's death, Ron Joyce helped create the Tim Horton Children's Camps and the Tim Horton Children's Foundation. He received many awards for his business success and charity work. In 1992, he was named a member of the Order of Canada for helping underprivileged children and young people.

The federal cabinet or government in Germany is led by the federal chancellor and includes other ministers. Their structure, how they are chosen, and when they can be removed are described in laws 62 to 69 of Germany's Basic Law. Unlike before, the Bundestag can only remove the chancellor with a special "no-confidence" vote, which also chooses a new chancellor. This ensures the whole cabinet stays together. This was done to avoid another dictatorship and a political crisis where no new chancellor could be chosen. If the chancellor loses a regular vote of confidence, they can ask the president to call an early election or declare a state of emergency, but the president is not forced to agree. Cabinet members can also be members of the Bundestag, and most are.

Sash! is a German DJ. His third studio album, Trilenium, came out on May 22, 2000, through the X-It label. People thought the album would be great, but it didn't do as well as expected. It only reached number 13 in the British album charts.

Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany (full name: Leopold George Duncan Albert), was born on April 7, 1853, and died on March 28, 1884, at age 30. He was the eighth child and youngest son of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. Prince Leopold was given the titles Duke of Albany, Earl of Clarence, and Baron Arklow. He had a condition called haemophilia, which caused his death.

Joan Blondell, born on August 30, 1906, and passed away on December 25, 1979, was an American actress who worked in films and on TV for about 50 years. She started her career in vaudeville. After winning a beauty pageant, she began her film career. Blondell became known for her funny, sexy roles with Warner Bros. She appeared in over 100 movies and TV shows. She was most active in films during the 1930s and early 1940s. During that time, she acted with Glenda Farrell in nine films, where they played gold diggers together. She continued acting in small roles on film and TV until the end of her life. In 1951, she was nominated for an Academy Award for her role in "The Blue Veil." Near the end of her life, she was nominated for a Golden Globe for her role in "Opening Night" in 1977. She also starred in "Grease" in 1978 and "The Champ" in 1979, shortly before her death from leukemia.

Roderick "Rody" Falesca Rene Trygvae Rijnders was a coxswain from the Netherlands. He was born on March 1, 1941, and died on January 15, 2018. Rody won a silver medal in the coxed pairs at the 1968 Summer Olympics, together with Hadriaan van Nes and Herman Suselbeek. He also got a bronze medal at the European level in 1965.

Bamba is a peanut butter-flavored snack made by the Osem Corporation in Kiryat Gat, Israel. Bamba is one of the top snack foods in Israel. It has been sold since 1964 and its sales have not gone down. Bamba takes up 25% of the Israeli snack market. Other similar snacks are Parpar from Telma (which became part of Unilever in 2000) and Shush from Strauss-Elite.

Fruitafossor was a small termite-eating mammal that lived in North America about 150 million years ago. It was found in Fruita, Colorado, on March 31, 2005. The animal was about the size of a chipmunk and looked like an armadillo or an anteater. It probably ate termites in a similar way to how anteaters do today. However, its skeleton showed that Fruitafossor was not related to armadillos, anteaters, or any other modern mammals. This suggests that the ability to eat ants or termites evolved independently many times in mammals, including in Fruitafossor, anteaters, numbats, aardwolves, aardvarks, pangolins, and echidnas.

Samuel Cornelius Phillips was born on January 5, 1923, and died on July 30, 2003. He was an American record producer who helped develop rock and roll in the 1950s. Phillips founded Sun Records and Sun Studio in Memphis, Tennessee. At Sun Studio, he worked with famous musicians like Elvis Presley, Roy Orbison, Jerry Lee Lewis, Carl Perkins, Johnny Cash, and Howlin' Wolf. He started Elvis Presley's career in 1954. In 1969, Phillips sold Sun Records to Shelby Singleton. Phillips also invested in the Holiday Inn hotel chain. He owned and managed radio stations in Memphis, Florence, Alabama, and Lake Worth, Florida. Phillips supported racial equality and helped break down racial barriers in the music industry.

Aleksandar Stipčević was born on October 10, 1930, and passed away on September 1, 2015. He was a Croatian archeologist, librarian, and historian who studied the Illyrians. His most important book, "Iliri" (which means "The Illyrians"), was published in 1974. This book was also translated into English, Italian, and Albanian.
Dillingen is a "landkreis" (district) in Swabia, Bavaria, Germany. It is next to the districts of Donau-Ries, Augsburg, and Günzburg. It also borders the Heidenheim district in Baden-Württemberg.

Amol is a city and the main city of Amol County in Mazandaran Province, Iran. The 2006 census showed that the city had 197,470 people living in 55,183 families. Amol is by a river called Haraz and is close to the Caspian Sea and the Alborz Mountains. It is about west of Tehran and south of the provincial capital, Sari. Amol is one of the oldest cities in Iran and is known for its history, culture, and industry. It is also famous for its rice production and is called the "city that does not die" and the "history, science, and philosophy city."

Aberfoyle is a village in Scotland. It is in the historic and registration county of Perthshire, and now part of the council area of Stirling. Aberfoyle is northwest of Glasgow. The village's name comes from the parish of Aberfoyle, which had 1,065 people in 2011.

"Avatar: The Last Airbender" is an American animated TV show created by Michael Dante Dimartino and Bryan Konietzko. It started on February 21, 2005, on Nickelodeon with a one-hour premiere and ended with a two-hour movie on July 19, 2008. The series is divided into three seasons, each called a "book," and every episode is a "chapter." In the story, Aang, the main character, needs to learn to control four elements: water, earth, and fire. Each season has 20 episodes, except the third, which has 21. There are also two recap episodes and three "shorts." In the "Avatar: The Last Airbender" world, some people can control the four elements: air, water, earth, and fire. These people are called "benders." Only some people can bend one element, but the Avatar can control all four elements and talk to spirits. The Avatar is born in one nation and reborn in another following a pattern: air, water, earth, and fire. The series is set 100 years after the Fire Nation starts a war, killing all Airbenders and searching for the Avatar, Aang, who is now an Airbender. Aang, trapped in ice for 100 years, doesn't know about the war. The show starts when Aang, accidentally freed by Katara, a Waterbender, begins his journey with his friends, Sokka, Katara, and later Toph and Zuko. Aang tries to learn all four elements and defeat the Fire Nation. Zuko, a Fire Nation prince, is also a main character. He was hurt in a fight with his father and wants to capture Aang to regain his father's favor and restore his honor.

Delphi, formerly known as Pytho, was a rich ancient sanctuary where the Pythia, an oracle, provided advice on important decisions. The ancient Greeks believed the center of the world was in Delphi, marked by a stone monument called the Omphalos. Delphi is on the southwest side of Mount Parnassus, looking down on the plain to the south and the valley of Phocis. Today, it is a large archaeological site with a small modern town nearby. UNESCO recognized Delphi as a world heritage site because it had a big influence in the ancient world. Many important ancient Greek city-states built monuments there, showing their strong connection as a Hellenic community.

Mather Tower, also known as Lincoln Tower, is a tall building in Chicago, Illinois. It is located at 75 East Wacker Drive in the downtown area, near the Chicago River. People sometimes call it "the inverted spyglass" because it has an 18-story octagonal tower on top of a 24-story rectangular building. Completed in 1928, it was the tallest building in Chicago at that time. The tower is very slender, with the least square footage per floor in Chicago. The building was designed by Herbert H. Riddle for the Mather Stock Car Company, which made rail cars for transporting animals. It was influenced by Chicago's 1923 zoning laws, which allowed tall, narrow buildings. The Mather family, the company's founder, is said to have influenced some of the building's design, including the octagonal tower. Plans for a second identical building on North Michigan Avenue were cancelled due to the Great Depression. By the 1990s, the building was in poor condition. In 2000, the top part, called the cupola, was removed due to safety concerns. Later that year, a new cupola was installed. Today, the lower part of the building is used as a hotel, and the upper part by a membership company. The building is now a Chicago historic landmark and has received national recognition for its preservation.

In telecommunications and computer networks, multiplexing is a way to combine multiple signals into one signal for sharing. This helps use a scarce resource more efficiently. For example, several phone calls can use one wire. Multiplexing started in the 1870s with telegraphy and is now common in communications. In telephony, George Owen Squier developed telephone carrier multiplexing in 1910. The multiplexed signal travels through a communication channel like a cable. This channel is divided into several logical channels, each for a different signal or data stream. On the receiving end, demultiplexing separates these original channels. A multiplexer (mux) does the combining, and a demultiplexer (demux or dmx) does the separating. Inverse multiplexing is the opposite. It splits one data stream into several, sends them over different channels, and then recombines them at the other end. In computing, I/O multiplexing can mean processing multiple input/output events using a single event loop, with system calls like poll and select in Unix.

Buddy Boudreaux, a saxophone and clarinet player, was born on December 27, 1917, and passed away on June 13, 2015. He was a big band and jazz musician in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Since 1934, he directed and played in several bands that toured the southern United States. These bands brought famous performers to Baton Rouge. The State-Times newspaper said he was "the city's sound of big band." His bands performed with artists like Andy Williams, Bernadette Peters, and Dionne Warwick. He also helped open shows for Tony Bennett, Tony Orlando, and Bill Cosby. In 1998, he co-wrote "My Baton Rouge" with his barber, Michael T. Abadie. This song was declared the city's official song.
CAPIF is an Argentine organization that belongs to the IFPI. The IFPI represents the music industry in Argentina. CAPIF is a nonprofit group made up of both big and smaller record companies.

"The Two Cars in Every Garage and Three Eyes on Every Fish" is the fourth episode of the second season of "The Simpsons." It first aired on November 1, 1990, on the Fox network in the United States. In the episode, Bart catches a three-eyed fish in a river near the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. When the plant is inspected, it is found to have many safety problems. Mr. Burns decides to run for governor to avoid closing the plant. The night before the election, Burns has a televised dinner with the Simpson family to show he cares about regular people. Marge sabotages Burns’s campaign by serving him the head of Blinky, the three-eyed fish. The episode, written by Sam Simon and John Swartzwelder and directed by Wes Archer, was supposed to be the season premiere. However, it was replaced with "Bart Gets an 'F'" because Bart was very popular in the early 1990s. The episode has references to several American films, mostly from 1941's "Citizen Kane," where Burns acts like Charles Foster Kane. Mary Bailey’s name is similar to George Bailey’s wife from "It's a Wonderful Life." People say the episode makes fun of American politics and environmental issues. It won an Environmental Media Award in 1991 for being the best TV episode with an environmental message. Since it first came out, Blinky the three-eyed fish has been mentioned in news about nuclear waste and mutations. Critics thought the episode was good because it made fun of American politics. It had a high Nielsen rating and was the most popular show on Fox that week.

June Gable was born on June 5, 1945. She is an American actress known for playing a character named Estelle Leonard, who was Joey's agent in the TV show "Friends." She was also nominated for a Tony Award for her work on Broadway.
James Rempe was born on November 4, 1947, in Scranton, Pennsylvania, USA. He is an American professional pool player. He was inducted into the Billiard Congress of America's Hall of Fame in 2002.

Raiford Chatman "Ossie" Davis was an American actor, director, poet, playwright, author, and civil rights activist. He was born on December 18, 1917, and died on February 4, 2005. Ossie Davis was married to Ruby Dee until his death. They often performed together. Both Ossie and Ruby were honored with the NAACP Image Awards Hall of Fame. They also received the National Medal of Arts and the Kennedy Center Honors. Ossie Davis was inducted into the American Theater Hall of Fame in 1994.
Helensburgh Football Club was a Scottish team from Helensburgh. They were part of the Scottish Football League Third Division from 1923 to 1926.

Addison Mitchell McConnell Jr. was born on February 20, 1942. He is an American politician and currently serves as Kentucky's senior U.S. senator. He is also the Senate Majority Leader. McConnell is the second Kentuckian to lead a Senate party, and he has the longest tenure among U.S. senators from Kentucky and U.S. Senate Republican leaders. McConnell was first elected to the Senate in 1984 and has been re-elected five times since. In 1998 and 2000, he was the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. He became Majority Whip in the 108th Congress and was re-elected in 2004. In 2006, he was elected Senate Minority Leader, a position he held until 2015. In 2015, when Republicans gained control of the Senate, McConnell became Senate Majority Leader. Early in his career, McConnell was known as a pragmatist and moderate Republican. However, he moved towards the right over time. He opposed stricter campaign finance laws and was involved in a 2010 Supreme Court ruling that partially overturned the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (McCain-Feingold). During the Obama administration, McConnell worked to stop major presidential initiatives, often used the filibuster, and blocked several of President Obama's judicial nominees, including Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland. Under McConnell's leadership during the Trump administration, Senate Republicans broke records for confirming judicial nominees, including Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh, who both joined the Supreme Court.

ReactOS is a free and open-source operating system for personal computers. It can run on computers with AMD64 or i686 processors. ReactOS is designed to work with programs and device drivers made for Windows Server 2003 and newer Windows versions. Some people think ReactOS could be a good replacement for Windows. ReactOS has been in development since 1996. It is not yet complete, so it is only recommended for testing and evaluation. However, many Windows programs, like Adobe Reader 6.0 and OpenOffice, currently work on ReactOS. ReactOS is mainly written in C, but some parts, such as the file explorer, are written in C++. The operating system includes some Windows API functionality. ReactOS has been adapted to run on AMD64 processors. ReactOS is part of the free and open-source (FOSS) community. It uses and works with other FOSS projects, especially the Wine project. Wine provides a way for Unix-like systems to run Windows programs.

Cosimo II de' Medici was born on May 12, 1590, and died on February 28, 1621. He became the Grand Duke of Tuscany in 1609 and ruled until his death. He was the older son of Ferdinando I de' Medici and Christina of Lorraine. For most of his twelve-year rule, he let his ministers handle the government. He is known for being Galileo Galilei's patron, as Galileo was his childhood teacher.

Afrikan tähti, known as the Star of Africa in Finnish and as the Missing Diamond in Swedish, is a Finnish board game designed by Kari Mannerla in 1951. It has been very popular in the Nordic countries for decades. The game was first published in Helsinki, Finland, in 1951. Kari Mannerla got inspired by stories about the world's largest diamond and created the game. He used a map of Africa to pick interesting places and drew random land, sea, and air routes. One of the game's innovations was that players could choose their own route instead of following a fixed path. Another was the use of tokens that were shuffled and placed randomly on the board, keeping players unsure about what they would find. Robbers and horseshoes were included to add excitement. Afrikan tähti was Kari Mannerla's last game. He was already an experienced 19-year-old game designer when he created it and knew it was special. He offered it to a publishing company, Tilgmann. After some negotiations, they agreed to print 10,000 copies and paid a modest amount. Mannerla insisted on negotiating any future prints separately. This turned out to be a good idea, as the game was more successful than expected. Over the next seven years, 100,000 games were sold, a record even today. Afrikan tähti has remained one of the best-selling board games in Finland for 65 years. It has been translated into over 16 languages and is most popular in the Nordic countries. It is called the Missing Diamond in Sweden and Norway, and the Star of Africa in Denmark. In Finland, over two million games have been sold, and nearly one million in Sweden and Norway. More than half a million have been sold in Denmark, with over 4.5 million games sold internationally. In his retirement, Kari Mannerla revived his old game Inkan Aarre, which sold over 100,000 copies in Finland. Both games are now directly copyrighted to Mannerla's five daughters.

The Teruel Cathedral, also known as Catedral de Santa María de Medialvilla de Teruel, is a Catholic church in Teruel, a city in the province of Aragon, Spain. It is dedicated to Saint Mary and is an example of Mudéjar architecture. It, along with other churches in Teruel and in the province of Zaragoza, was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

Romance is an emotional feeling of love for another person or a strong attraction towards them. People show their feelings through courtship behaviors. The "Wiley Blackwell Encyclopedia of Family Studies" says that romantic love, based on mutual attraction and a connection between two people, can change family and marriage models. This means romantic love can start the attraction between two people. Romantic love was mainly used in Western countries after the 1800s. It is important for starting an intimate relationship and building a family. "Collins Dictionary" defines romantic love as a very intense and idealized love relationship where the other person is seen as having great virtues and beauty, making the relationship more important than other considerations, including material ones. Romantic feelings can exist without expecting physical attraction, and they can be expressed in various ways. Historically, the term "romance" comes from the medieval ideal of chivalry found in chivalric romance literature.

Paiçandu is a city in the state of Paraná in southern Brazil. It was founded in 1948 and became an independent municipality on November 19, 1960. In 2015, the population was 39,291 people. The city covers an area of 171.4 square kilometers.

Alfred was the second son of Edward, who was also known as Edward the Elder. Alfred was born around 902 and died on August 2, 924. He was born to Edward's second wife, Aelflaed, after Edward's first wife.

An inventor is someone who creates or discovers something new, like a method, a device, or a useful thing. The term "inventor" comes from the Latin word "invenire," meaning "to find." Patents are given to encourage inventors. They grant a limited-time, exclusive right to use their inventions if the inventions are new, not obvious, and useful. While inventing is related to science and engineering, inventors don't have to be engineers or scientists.
Dastilbe was a type of ancient fish from a long time ago. It belongs to a group called bony fish. It lived during the Aptian period.

Netball is a ball game played by two teams of seven players. It's most popular in Commonwealth countries, especially in schools, and is mainly played by women. More than 20 million people play netball in over 80 countries. Major domestic leagues include the Netball Superleague in Great Britain, Suncorp Super Netball in Australia, and the ANZ Premiership in New Zealand. Four main international competitions are the World Netball Championships, the Commonwealth Games, and the annual Quad Series and Fast5 Series. Netball became an international Olympic Committee-recognized sport in 1995 but hasn't been included in the Olympics. Games are played on a rectangular court with goal rings at each end. Teams try to score by passing the ball and shooting it through the goal ring. Players have specific positions, limiting where they can move on the court. In play, a player with the ball can hold it for only three seconds before shooting or passing. The winning team scores the most goals. A netball game lasts 60 minutes. Variations have been made to make the game faster and more appealing. Netball began in England in the 1890s, derived from early basketball versions. By 1960, international rules were set, and the International Netball Federation (INF) was formed. As of 2019, the INF includes over 70 national teams in five global regions.
There is an art museum in Kyoto, Japan. It is also known as MOMAK, which stands for Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto.

The Škoda Fabia is a supermini car made by the Czech company Škoda Auto since 1999. It replaced the Škoda Felicia, which stopped being made in 2001. When it first came out, the Fabia was available in hatchback, estate (called Fabia Combi), and saloon (called Fabia Sedan) versions. Since 2007, only hatchback and estate versions have been offered. The third generation Fabia was introduced in 2015.

The national flag of Anguilla, a British overseas territory, has a blue background with the British flag in the top-left corner. In the right part of the flag, there are three dolphins forming a circle, representing friendship, wisdom, and strength. The white color stands for peace, and the blue color represents the sea, as well as ideas of faith, youth, and hope. This is Anguilla’s third flag, after previous ones like a red flag with a yellow island name and two mermaids, or a similar red or purple flag without the name. People didn't like the first flag and replaced it with a dolphin flag during a short period of independence. This dolphin flag was white with a blue band at the bottom and three golden dolphins. The blue ensign was adopted in 1990 and is used on land and by government ships. The red ensign, used by civilian ships, is common throughout the British Empire. Anguilla doesn't have a special red ensign. The dolphin flag is often used as a general civil flag. The governor uses a flag with the Anguilla coat of arms on the Union Jack.

Badfinger was a Welsh/English rock band formed in Swansea. They were active from the 1960s to the 1980s. Their main members were Pete Ham, Mike Gibbins, Tom Evans, and Joey Molland. The band was known for its influence on 1970s power pop music. Badfinger started as a group called The Ivys, formed in 1961. In 1968, they became the first band signed by Apple Records, the label started by The Beatles. They changed their name to Badfinger, inspired by the title of The Beatles' 1967 song "With a Little Help from My Friends," which they called "Bad Finger Boogie." From 1968 to 1973, Badfinger recorded five albums and toured a lot. They had four big hits between 1970 and 1972: "Come and Get It," "No Matter What," "Day After Day," and "Baby Blue." Their song "Without You" was popular too and became a hit for Harry Nilsson and Mariah Carey many years later. After Apple Records closed in 1973, Badfinger faced many problems like legal and financial issues. In 1975, Pete Ham took his own life. The remaining members tried to keep the band going but faced more issues. Joey Molland and Tom Evans often had conflicts. Their later albums didn't do well. In 1983, Tom Evans also took his own life.
Challis is the biggest city in Custer County, Idaho, United States. It is also the county seat. In 2010, the population was 1,081, which was more than in 2000, when it was 909.

In physics, chemistry, and electronic engineering, an electron hole is the absence of an electron in a position where one could exist in an atom or lattice. While not a particle, a hole acts like a positively charged particle. Since atoms or crystal lattices normally have a balance of charges, the absence of an electron creates a positive charge. Holes can move through a metal or semiconductor crystal lattice, just like electrons, and they are crucial in the operation of semiconductor devices such as transistors, diodes, and integrated circuits. When an electron is excited to a higher state, it leaves behind a hole. This concept is used in Auger electron spectroscopy and other x-ray techniques. Holes also help explain why electrons don't scatter much in crystals, like metals and semiconductors. In crystal structures, calculations of electronic band structure give an effective negative mass to electrons at the top of a band. However, it is easier to understand the concept by considering a positive charge with a positive mass in these situations.

Bob Kelly Abreu, born on March 11, 1974, is a former baseball player from Venezuela. People call him "El Comedulce" and "La Leche." He played as an outfielder in Major League Baseball (MLB) for the Houston Astros, Philadelphia Phillies, New York Yankees, Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim, Los Angeles Dodgers, and New York Mets. Abreu is a two-time All-Star. He won a Rawlings Gold Glove Award and a Silver Slugger Award. He played in more games than anyone else in a single season twice. He also had the most doubles and triples. As of 2014, Abreu led all active players in doubles (565), walks (1,456), and outfield assists (136). He was fifth in runs scored (1,441) and stolen bases (400), seventh in extra-base hits (911), and on-base percentage (0.396), and tenth in runs batted in (1,363).

Known for his strict rule over Manchukuo, a Japanese puppet state in northeast China, Kishi was called "devil of Shōwa." After World War II, Kishi was imprisoned for three years as a suspect in Class A war crimes. However, the U.S. government released him, thinking he was the best person to lead post-war Japan towards an American-friendly direction. In the 1950s, Kishi worked to strengthen Japan's conservative parties against the Japan Socialist Party. He is credited with helping to start the "1955 system," a period when the Liberal Democratic Party was the dominant political party in Japan.

Antonín Dvořák, born on September 8, 1841, and died on May 1, 1904, was a Czech composer. He was one of the first to gain worldwide fame. Dvořák often used rhythms and aspects of Moravian and Bohemian folk music in his works, following the example of his predecessor, Bedřich Smetana. People described his style as combining a national style with the symphonic tradition, effectively using folk influences. Dvořák showed his musical talent early. He started playing the violin well at six years old. His first public performances were in Prague in 1872 and 1873. In 1874, he entered a competition in Germany with his first symphony but didn't win. The manuscript was lost until found decades later. In 1874, 1876, and 1877, he won the Austrian state prize for composition. Johannes Brahms and Eduard Hanslick, members of the jury, came to know him. Brahms introduced Dvořák to his publisher, Simrock, who commissioned the "Slavonic Dances," which were well-received. This launched Dvořák's international reputation. In 1880, Dvořák composed his first religious work, "Stabat Mater," which was performed in Prague and then in London in 1883, leading to more performances in the UK and the US. He made nine visits to England, often conducting his own works. He wrote his seventh symphony for London. In 1890, he visited Russia and conducted his music in Moscow and Saint Petersburg. In 1891, Dvořák became a professor at the Prague Conservatory. He wrote the "Dumky Trio" in 1890–91, a successful chamber music piece. In 1892, he moved to the United States, becoming the director of the National Conservatory of Music in New York City. There, he composed his most famous works: the "New World Symphony," which gained worldwide fame, and his Cello Concerto, widely considered one of the best cello concertos. He also wrote the "American String Quartet" during this time. Short payments and homesickness made him leave the US and return to Bohemia in 1895. All of Dvořák's nine operas, except the first, have Czech librettos and were meant to showcase Czech national spirit. His most successful opera is "Rusalka." Popular among his smaller works are the "Humoresque" and the song "Songs My Mother Taught Me." He is described as one of the most versatile composers of his time.

The Imja Khola is a river that joins the Dudh Kosi in Nepal. It comes from the slopes near Mount Everest. The Khumbu Glacier feeds the Lobujya River, which becomes the Imja Khola. The Imja Khola then flows south to meet the Dudh Kosi at Tengboche. The Imja Khola gets water from the Imja Glacier through the Dingboche Valley.

Before the 1980s, cameras used tubes to capture images, similar to a TV screen. These tubes, known as cathode ray tubes, were used in cameras from the early 1930s until the 1980s. In these tubes, a ray scanned across the image, creating a signal based on the image's brightness. The ray was very small compared to the image, allowing about 483 lines in NTSC format or 576 lines in PAL format.

"Sunday Bloody Sunday" is a song by Irish rock band U2. It was the first track on their 1983 album "War" and came out as the album's third single on March 21, 1983, in the Netherlands and West Germany. The song is known for its strong beat, loud guitar, and pleasant melodies. One of U2's most political songs, it talks about the sad events of Bloody Sunday in Derry in 1972, where British soldiers hurt innocent people who were peacefully protesting. Along with "New Year's Day," this song helped U2 become more popular. Critics liked it when it was first released. The song is a main part of U2's live shows. In early performances, it caused some controversy. But Bono, the lead singer, kept reminding people about the message against violence. Today, it is one of U2's most famous songs. Many people think it is one of the best protest songs ever. Over a dozen artists have covered it. "Rolling Stone" magazine ranked it as the 272nd-best song of all time.

Fort Scott is a city in Bourbon County, Kansas, United States. It is south of Kansas City and located near the Marmaton River. In 2010, there were 8,087 people living there. The city is home to the Fort Scott National Historic Site and the Fort Scott National Cemetery. Fort Scott is named after General Winfield Scott.
Ernie is a boy's name. Sometimes it is a shorter version of Ernest. It could mean:
Moutiers-sur-le-Lay is a commune in Vendée, which is in the Pays de la Loire region of western France.

Eli Lilly and Company is an American pharmaceutical company based in Indianapolis, Indiana. It has offices in 18 countries and sells products in about 125 countries. The company was founded in 1876 by Eli Lilly, a chemist and Civil War veteran. Some of its important achievements include producing the first mass-produced polio vaccine and insulin. Lilly was one of the first to use recombinant DNA to make human insulin, including Humalog and Humulin, and the first approved biosimilar insulin product in the US, Basaglar. Lilly makes many psychiatric medications, such as Prozac, Dolophine, Cymbalta, and Zyprexa. According to John Marks, the company also produced LSD for the CIA’s MKULTRA program. The company ranks 123rd on the 2019 Fortune 500 list and 221st on the Forbes Global 2000 list. It is also listed as one of America's best employers. Eli Lilly is a member of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America and the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations. In 1997, it was the largest corporation and the largest charitable benefactor in Indiana.

A penalty shootout decides a winner in games that are tied. The rules can be different for various sports and competitions. Usually, one player takes a shot from a specific spot, with only the goalkeeper as the defender. If the scores are still tied, players keep taking shots in turns. The team that scores without the other team scoring in between wins. This can go on until everyone has shot, and if it's still tied, extra shots are taken until one team scores and the other doesn't. It's also called "sudden death."

Kavala is a city in northern Greece. It is the main seaport in eastern Macedonia and the capital of the Kavala regional unit. Kavala is located on the Bay of Kavala, across from the island of Thasos. It is also on the Egnatia Motorway. From Kavala, it takes about one and a half hours to get to Thessaloniki, and about forty minutes to get to Drama or Xanthi. It is about 150 kilometers west of Alexandroupoli. Kavala is an important economic center in northern Greece. It is a place for commerce, tourism, fishing, and oil-related activities. In the past, Kavala was also known for trading tobacco.

Morissen was a former municipality in the district of Surselva, in the Swiss canton of Graubünden. On January 1, 2013, Morissen and seven other municipalities—Cumbel, Degen, Lumbrein, Suraua, Vignogn, Vella, and Vrin—merged into a new municipality called Lumnezia.
Marcy is a commune in Aisne, which is in Hauts-de-France, a region in northern France.

Hans Modrow, born on January 27, 1928, is a German politician. He was the last communist leader of East Germany. During the peaceful revolution, he became the acting leader in late 1989 and early 1990, trying to stop German reunification. After the fall of communism and reunification, Modrow was accused of election fraud and lying. In 1995, he was convicted by a court in Dresden. He was also the honorary leader of a party called the Party of Democratic Socialism and has been the president of the Left Party's Council of Elders since 2007.

In 1965, there was a funny American movie called "How to Murder Your Wife." It was made by United Artists. George Axelrod produced it, and Richard Quine directed it. Jack Lemmon, Virna Lisi, and Terry-Thomas were the main actors. Richard Quine also directed Jack Lemmon in other films like "My Sister Eileen" and "It Happened to Jane." The funny drawings in the movie were by Mel Keefer. He drew comic strips for newspapers, such as "Perry Mason" and "Mac Divot." Alex Toth made a short comic strip in Mel Keefer's style. It was shown in "The Hollywood Reporter" and some newspapers to promote the movie before it opened in theaters.
Hiroshi Umemura, born on February 22, 1972, is a Japanese mixed martial artist. He fought in the bantamweight and featherweight divisions.

Lynne Carol, born Josephine Caroline Gertrude Mary Faith Harber on June 29, 1914, and died on June 30, 1990, was an actress from Wales. She was often called Lynne Carol. She appeared mainly in TV series and telemovies. She was famous for playing Martha Longhurst in the soap opera "Coronation Street." Martha Longhurst was a busybody character. Lynne Carol played this role from the second episode in 1960 until 1964, when the character was removed from the show.
Newark is a city in Texas, in Tarrant and Wise counties. The population was 1,005 according to the 2010 census.

In math, the lowest common denominator, or LCD, is the smallest number that can be evenly divided by the denominators of several fractions. It helps make adding, subtracting, and comparing fractions easier.

A prefix is a word part added to the start of another word. For example, adding "un-" to "happy" makes "unhappy." In language study, a prefix can also be called a preformative because it changes the word's form. Prefixes can be inflectional or derivational. Inflectional prefixes make a word's form different but keep the same basic meaning and category. Derivational prefixes create new words with new meanings and can change word categories. Prefixes are usually bound morphemes. In English, there are no inflectional prefixes; instead, suffixes are used for that purpose. The word "prefix" itself comes from "fix" (meaning "attach") and "pre-" (meaning "before"), both from Latin.

The Lamborghini Huracán is a sports car made by Lamborghini, an Italian car company. It replaced the Gallardo, which had a V10 engine. The Huracán first showed to the world at the 2014 Geneva Auto Show. It came out for sale in the second quarter of 2014. Its name means "hurricane" in Spanish. The car has 610 metric horsepower and four-wheel drive. LP in its name stands for "longitudinale posteriore," which means the engine is in the middle of the car, towards the back.

Suwanee is a city in Gwinnett County, Georgia. In 2010, it had 15,355 people. By 2019, the population grew to about 20,907. From 1979 to 2001, the Atlanta Falcons played their home games in Suwanee. In 2007, Suwanee was named one of the top 10 places to live by Money magazine. In 2012, Kiplinger named Suwanee the third-best place in America for raising families. In 2013, Family Circle magazine listed Suwanee as one of the best towns for families in the country. In 2018, Niche rated Suwanee first for the best public schools in Georgia. Suwanee's zip code (30024) is used by parts of Forsyth and Fulton counties for mailing addresses.
Sajid Nawaz Khan was born on March 25, 1975. He is a Pakistani politician who was a member of Pakistan's National Assembly from June 2013 to May 2018.

Action Comics is an American comic book series. It introduced Superman, one of the first major superheroes. The company that published it was first called National Allied Publications. Later, it became known as National Comics Publications and National Periodical Publications. Now, it is called DC Comics. The first series of Action Comics came out in 1938 and ended in 2011, making it one of the longest-running comic books. In 2011, a second series of Action Comics started with issue number 1 and ended in 2016. In August 2016, the series returned to its original numbering with issue number 957.

Keitele is a large lake in central Finland. It covers 493.59 square kilometers and is the 9th largest lake in the country. The lake is divided into three parts: Ylä-, Keski-, and Ala-Keitele, with Keski-Keitele being the largest. The water is very clear and healthy. The towns of Äänekoski and Viitasaari are near the lake. The northern part of the lake is called Ylä-Keitele. Much of Ylä-Keitele is protected because of its clear water and natural state. In 1904, a famous Finnish painter named Akseli Gallen-Kallela worked at Lake Keitele during the summer. This was his third and most detailed painting of the lake. He showed it in Helsinki that same year. The painting is signed with his Swedish name, which he used later. He is known today as Akseli Gallen-Kallela. This painting is now in the National Gallery in London. The lake is also mentioned in a book called "A Corpse in the Koryo" by James Church, published in 2006.
The Centre Étienne Desmarteau is a multi-purpose complex in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. It has two ice rinks.

The Gaslight Anthem was an American rock band from New Brunswick, New Jersey. They formed in 2006. The band members are Brian Fallon (lead vocals, rhythm guitar), Alex Rosamilia (lead guitar, backing vocals), Alex Levine (bass guitar, backing vocals), and Benny Horowitz (drums, percussion). The band released their first album, "Sink or Swim," on Xoxo Records in May 2007. Their second album, "The '59 Sound," came out on SideOneDummy Records in August 2008. "American Slang" was released in June 2010, and "Handwritten" was released in July 2012 through Mercury Records. The lead single from "Handwritten," "45," was their most successful and well-known song. Their fifth album, "Get Hurt," was released on August 12, 2014, through Island Records. The band took an indefinite break after their European summer tour, which ended at the Reading Festival on August 30. They briefly reunited in 2018 to celebrate the 10th anniversary of "The '59 Sound" before taking another break.
