An anticyclonic storm is a weather storm where winds move in a clockwise direction around the storm. This is opposite to the direction of winds in a low-pressure area.

Usury is a practice where loans are given in an unfair way, making the lender richer than they should be. This can be seen as wrong or bad. In some cases, it means charging too much interest. In legal terms, usury is when interest is charged above the maximum rate allowed by law. A person who does this is called a usurer, or sometimes a loan shark in modern times. In ancient times, including in Christian, Jewish, and some Islamic societies, usury meant charging any interest on loans and was considered wrong. For example, in ancient India, there were rules stopping higher castes from doing usury. Religious texts from Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam also condemn usury. Some ancient societies, like Greece and Rome, banned loans with interest. During this time, the Catholic Church and other Protestant churches in medieval Europe believed charging any interest was sinful, including fees for using money. Charging interest was seen as a sin because it was believed to be unfair.

Wenatchee is a city in Washington, United States. It is the biggest city in Chelan County and its seat. In 2010, it had about 31,925 people. By 2019, an estimate said there were about 34,360 people. The city sits where the Columbia and Wenatchee rivers meet, near the Cascade Mountains. Wenatchee is on the west side of the Columbia River, opposite East Wenatchee. It is part of the Wenatchee–East Wenatchee area, which includes Chelan and Douglas counties and has about 110,884 people. People also call the land between Rocky Reach and Rock Island Dam the Wenatchee Valley area. Wenatchee got its name from the nearby Wenatchi Indian tribe. The name comes from a Sahaptin word meaning "river from canyons" or "rainbow robe." "Awenatchela" means "people at the river's source." Wenatchee is known as the "apple capital of the world" because it has many apple orchards. It's also sometimes called the "buckle of the power belt of the Great Northwest," a term referring to hydroelectric dams on the Columbia River. The city's newspaper, the Wenatchee World, uses this phrase at the top.

Charles Beauvau, Prince of Craon, was born on September 10, 1720, and died on May 21, 1793. He became the 2nd Prince of Craon in 1754 and was named Marshal of France in 1783. He was a French scholar, nobleman, and general. He was the son of Marc de Beauvau and brother of Madame de Boufflers. Through his sister, he was related to the poet Stanislas de Boufflers.

Mikhail Nikolayevich Zadornov, born on July 21, 1948, in Jurmala, Latvian SSR, USSR, passed away on November 10, 2017, in Moscow, Russia. He was a Soviet and Russian comedian and writer. Zadornov's father, Nikolai Zadornov, was a well-known writer from Riga. His mother, Elena Matusevich (1909-1992), came from an old noble family with roots going back to the Polish King Stephen Bathory. As a child, Zadornov would listen to his father read him adventure and suspense stories, and poems before bedtime. His parents wanted him to become an engineer, so he studied at an engineering institute. Mikhail Zadornov graduated from Moscow Aviation Institute. However, in the early 1980s, he began his career as a humorist and later humorously recalled his engineering studies.

Samuel Willenberg, who used the name Igo, was born on February 16, 1923, and died on February 19, 2016. He was a Polish Holocaust survivor, artist, and writer. During World War II, Willenberg worked as part of a special group called the "sonderkommando" at the Treblinka extermination camp. He was involved in a planned revolt there in August 1943. About 300 people escaped, and around 79 survived the war. After the revolt, Willenberg went to Warsaw. By the end of the war, he joined the Warsaw Uprising. At the time of his death, Willenberg was the last known survivor of the August 1943 revolt at Treblinka. Like many other survivors, Willenberg moved to Israel after the war. He received important awards from Poland, including the "Virtuti Militari" and the Commander's Cross of the Order of Merit, given by President Lech Kaczyński. His book, "Revolt in Treblinka," was published in Hebrew, Polish, and English between 1986 and 1991. He also created sculptures and paintings.

Richmond is a town in Washington County, Rhode Island. In 2010, it had 7, 708 people. It includes several villages: Alton, Arcadia, Barberville, Carolina, Hillsdale, Kenyon, Shannock, Tug Hollow, Usquepaug, Wood River Junction, Woodville, and Wyoming. Richmond's students go to the Chariho Regional School District.
Saint-Jean-sur-Verthe is a village in Ain, which is in eastern France.

Adobe Dreamweaver is a web development tool from Adobe Inc. It was first created by Macromedia in 1997 and continued to be developed by them until 2005 when Macromedia was acquired by Adobe. Dreamweaver can be used on both macOS and Windows. After Adobe bought Macromedia, newer versions of Dreamweaver better followed web standards set by the W3C. More recent versions have improved support for technologies like CSS, JavaScript, and server-side languages such as ASP, ColdFusion, and PHP.

Zalmoxes is an extinct genus of rhabdodontid ornithopod dinosaur from Romania. It was first named as "Mochlodon robustum" in 1899 by Franz Nopcsa. Later, it was reclassified as "Rhabdodon robustum" in 1915 by the same person. In 1990, the name was corrected to "Rhabdodon robustus." In 2003, it was reclassified again as the type species Zalmoxes robustus. The name "Zalmoxes" comes from the Dacian deity Zalmoxis, and "robustus" means the remains were strong. In 2003, another species, Zalmoxes shqiperorum, was named after Albanians.
Jalal Dabagh, born in 1939, is a Kurdish politician and writer.

Golf Mill Shopping Center, also called Golf Mill Center, is a mall in Niles, Illinois. Its address is 239 Golf Mill Center. The mall has over 100 stores and is managed by Sterling Retail Services. It is next to Golf Road (Illinois Route 58), Milwaukee Avenue (Illinois Route 21), and Greenwood Avenue. The mall includes JC Penney, Target, Kohl’s, Ross Dress for Less, AMC theatres, two grocery stores, an XSport fitness center, a nine-story office building, and other small businesses.

Wikimania is the official yearly meeting of the Wikimedia Foundation. At this event, people discuss and present topics like Wikipedia, other wikis, free knowledge, and open-source software. They also talk about the technical and social aspects related to these projects. Since 2011, the "Wikimedian of the Year" award is given at Wikimania. This event will be in Bangkok, Thailand in 2021. The planned event in August 2020 was delayed because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Saint-Trivier-de-Courtes is a town in Ain, which is in eastern France.

Giuseppe Zamberletti was born on December 17, 1933, and passed away on January 26, 2019. He was an Italian politician. Zamberletti helped start Italy's Civil Protection service. He became the first minister of Civil Protection in Italy in 1981.

Alanis Nadine Morissette, born on June 1, 1974, is a singer, songwriter, and actress from Canada. Known for her emotive mezzo-soprano voice, she started her career in the early 1990s with two dance-pop albums that didn't do very well. Later, she moved to Holmby Hills, Los Angeles, as part of a recording deal. In 1995, she released "Jagged Little Pill," a rock-oriented album that sold over 33 million copies worldwide and is her most famous work. Her next album, "Supposed Former Infatuation Junkie," came out in 1998. After that, Morissette took control of her creative work and produced several albums, including "Under Rug Swept" (2002), "So-Called Chaos" (2004), "Flavors of Entanglement" (2008), and "Havoc and Bright Lights" (2012). Her ninth album, "Such Pretty Forks in the Road," was released in 2020. She has sold over 75 million records worldwide and is called the "queen of alt-rock angst" by Rolling Stone.

Shah Azizur Rahman was a politician from Bangladesh. He served as the prime minister of Bangladesh. However, he faced a lot of controversy because he worked with the Pakistan army against those trying to form Bangladesh.

A parameter is a characteristic that helps define or classify a system, like an event, project, or object. It is useful for identifying the system or evaluating its status. The word comes from ancient Greek, where "para" means "beside" or " subsidiary," and "metron" means "measure." In general, parameters are important elements in a system. In specific fields like math, computer programming, engineering, and statistics, parameters have more precise meanings. Sometimes people use "parameter" instead of "limit" or "boundary" in casual talk, which might come from mixing up the idea of "perimeter."

A mirage is a natural optical phenomenon where light bends, making distant objects or the sky look displaced. The word "mirage" comes from the Latin "mirari," meaning "to look at" or "to wonder at." There are three types of mirages: inferior, superior, and fata morgana. Inferior mirages appear lower and are easily mistaken for water on land. Superior mirages are higher, and fata morgana create multiple, stacked images that change quickly. Unlike hallucinations, mirages are real and can be photographed because light rays bend to form the image at the observer's location. However, what the image represents depends on how our minds interpret it.

Tom Pevsner was born on October 2, 1926, and died on August 18, 2014. He was a British assistant film director and producer who worked for over 40 years. He was the second of three children, born to Sir Nikolaus Pevsner, an architectural historian of Russian-Jewish background. The family moved from Germany to the UK in 1933 to avoid the Nazis. After serving in the British Army from 1944 to 1948, Pevsner studied modern languages at Cambridge University. There, he was part of the St. John's College Film Society and edited "The Cambridge Review." After graduating, he worked at the Film Finance Corporation. Pevsner worked on many films, including "The Ladykillers" (1955), "The Longest Day" (1962), and "The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes" (1970) as an assistant director. He also produced "Dracula." He became an associate and then executive producer for every James Bond film from "For Your Eyes Only" to "GoldenEye." His work on the Bond films was recognized in "Spectre," where character Q mentions Pevsner. Pevsner was 87 when he died. He was remembered in the "In Memoriam" tribute during the 2015 Academy Awards.

Richard Church Thompson, born on October 8, 1957, and passed away on July 27, 2016, was an American illustrator and cartoonist. He is famous for his comic strip "Cul de Sac" and the illustrated poem "Make the Pie Higher." In 2010, he won the Reuben Award for the best cartoonist.

The Nelson Mandela Bridge is in Johannesburg, South Africa. It is one of five bridges that cross railway lines just west of Johannesburg Park Station. The first bridge is the Johan Rissik Bridge, next to the station. The Nelson Mandela Bridge was finished in 2003 and cost R38 million. The bridge was built to connect two important business areas, Braamfontein and Newtown, and to make the inner city better and more modern. It is part of the M27 route in Johannesburg.

The Hateful Eight, sometimes called The H8ful Eight, is a 2015 Western movie by Quentin Tarantino. It stars Samuel L. Jackson, Kurt Russell, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Walton Goggins, Demian Bichir, Tim Roth, Michael Madsen, and Bruce Dern. The story is about eight strangers who seek shelter from a blizzard at a stagecoach stop after the American Civil War. Tarantino announced the movie in November 2013. He first planned it as a novel and a sequel to Django Unchained (2012), but changed it into a standalone film. After the script leaked in January 2014, Tarantino cancelled it and did a live reading. He later decided to make the movie again. Filming began on December 8, 2014, near Telluride, Colorado. The movie has Italian composer Ennio Morricone's first and only score for a Tarantino film. It was released on December 25, 2015, in a limited roadshow release on 70mm film, and expanded to theaters on December 30, 2015. Critics liked Leigh's performance and Morricone's score. The movie made $155.8 million. The budget was estimated between $44 million to $62 million. Morricone won an Oscar for best original score and a Golden Globe for his work. The film also got nominations for best supporting actress and best cinematography. On April 25, 2019, the movie was re-released as a four-episode miniseries on Netflix. This was Tarantino's last film with the Weinstein Company, as he ended his working relationship after sexual abuse allegations against Harvey Weinstein in October 2017.

Mason is a city in Michigan, a U.S. state. It got its name from the state's first governor, Stevens T. Mason. In 2010, the city had 8, 252 people. Mason is a county seat in Ingham County. It is special because it is the only city that is a county seat but not a state capital. The state capital, Lansing, is also in Ingham County. Even though Mason is the county seat, many county offices and courtrooms are in Lansing.
Ambleny is a commune in the Aisne department, which is in the Hauts-de-France region of northern France. The people who live there are called Amblenois or Amblenoises.

Natural Steps is an unincorporated place in Pulaski County, Arkansas, United States. It is 18 miles northwest of Little Rock, along the southern side of the Arkansas River, on Arkansas Highway 300. In 2010, it had 426 people. Today, it is a small farming community with some businesses. Most of the Natural Steps, a geologic formation, still exist and are used as a marker for river runners. These Natural Steps are not open to the public for viewing.

The cochlea is part of the inner ear and helps us hear. It is a spiral tube in the bony labyrinth, making 2.75 turns in humans. The modiolus is the center of this spiral. Inside the cochlea, there is a key part called the organ of Corti, which is where we sense sounds. This organ is found on the wall that separates the fluid-filled chambers. The name "cochlea" comes from this description.

Myrtle "Kay" Thompson Cagle lived from June 3, 1925, to December 22, 2019. She was an American pilot and part of the Mercury 13 group of female astronauts. She worked as a flight instructor and wrote about aviation in North Carolina.

In American history, the fire-eaters were pro-slavery Democrats in the south before the Civil War. They wanted the southern states to separate and form a new country. This new country became known as the Confederate States of America. Robert Barnwell Rhett from South Carolina was the leader. Some fire-eaters wanted to bring back America's involvement in the slave trade in the Atlantic, which was illegal since 1808.

Daniel Michael Devito Jr., born on November 17, 1944, is an American actor, comedian, director, producer, and writer. He became famous for playing Louie De Palma, a taxi dispatcher, in the TV show "Taxi" from 1978 to 1983. This role earned him a Golden Globe and an Emmy award. He also acts as Frank Reynolds in the TV sitcom "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia," which started in 2006. Devito has acted in many movies, including "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest" (1975), "Twins" (1988), and "Matilda" (1996). He has also voiced characters in movies like "Space Jam" (1996) and "The Lorax" (2012). He and Michael Shamberg started Jersey Films. Stacey Sher later joined them as an equal partner. Jersey Films produced popular movies like "Pulp Fiction," "Garden State," and "Freedom Writers." Devito owned Jersey Television, which made the comedy show "Reno 911!" with him and his wife, Rhea Perlman, starring together in the 1996 film "Matilda," based on Roald Dahl's book. Devito was nominated for an Academy Award as a producer for "Erin Brockovich." Devito is shorter than average because of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, a rare genetic condition that affects bone growth.
Reid is an Australian electoral district in New South Wales.
Auguste Chabaud was a French artist who lived from October 3, 1882, to May 23, 1955. He made paintings and sculptures.

The 1978 FIFA World Cup, the 11th tournament, was in Argentina from June 1 to June 25. Argentina won, beating the Netherlands 3-1 in extra time in the final. The final was at the River Plate stadium in Buenos Aires. This was Argentina's first World Cup win, making them the fifth team to host and win the tournament, after Uruguay, Italy, England, and West Germany. Argentina, the Netherlands, and Brazil were the top three. Iran and Tunisia played their first World Cup. This was the last time 16 teams played. From 1930 to 2002, only 15 teams (plus the host) could enter. For the next World Cup in Spain, FIFA increased the number of teams to 24. The official ball was the Adidas Tango.

Healesville Sanctuary, formerly called Sir Colin Mackenzie Sanctuary, is a zoo that focuses on native Australian animals. It's in Healesville, a rural area in Victoria, Australia. The zoo has a history of breeding native animals and is one of two places that have successfully bred a platypus. The other is Sydney's Taronga Zoo. It also helps with breeding endangered helmeted honeyeaters. The zoo is set in a natural bushland. Paths wind through different areas, showing wallabies, wombats, dingoes, kangaroos, and over 200 native bird species. Visitors can take guided tours, watch bird shows, and get information.
pré-en-pail was a former commune in Mayenne, a department in northwest France. On January 1, 2016, it became part of a new commune called pré-en-pail-saint-samson.

Aerospace France (3AF or AAAF) is the French national organization for people who work or have an interest in airplanes and space. It is based in Paris and was formed in 1971 from two earlier groups. The first, the "French Association of Aerospace Engineers and Technicians" (AFITAE), started in 1945. The second, the "French Society of Astronautics" (SFA), began in 1955. 3AF helps people in the aerospace industry share their ideas and promote science and technology related to space and aviation. Most of its members are engineers and scientists. Big companies like Alcatel Space, EADS, and Arianespace are part of 3AF. The organization also has special members called honorary members. 3AF is part of a bigger group called the Confederation of European Aerospace Societies (CEAS). This group includes other similar organizations from Germany, Britain, and Italy.

Fermentation is a process where enzymes cause chemical changes in organic materials. In biochemistry, it specifically means extracting energy from sugars without using oxygen. In food production, it refers to microorganisms making desired changes to foods or drinks. The study of fermentation is called zymology. In microorganisms, fermentation creates energy by breaking down nutrients without oxygen. People have been using fermentation to make food and drinks since ancient times. For example, fermentation makes lactic acid in foods like pickles, kombucha, kimchi, and yogurt. It also helps create alcoholic drinks like wine and beer. Fermentation happens in the digestive systems of all animals, including humans.

Arif-Ur-Rehman Alvi was born on August 29, 1949. He is a politician from Pakistan. Alvi became the 13th president of Pakistan on September 9, 2018. He was a member of Pakistan's National Assembly from June 2013 to May 2018 and again from August to September 2018. Alvi is a founding member of Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI). He became Pakistan's president after winning the presidential election on September 4, 2018.

Maynard Elliott Solomon, born on January 5, 1930, is a co-founder of Vanguard Records. He also worked as a music producer. Recently, he has written biographies about Viennese classical composers. His work includes a significant biography about Beethoven and a collection of essays also about Beethoven. He also wrote a biography about Mozart. Solomon was the first to openly suggest that Schubert might have been homosexual in a scholarly way.
Lancaster can mean: A town A county

Potsdam is the biggest city in the German state of Brandenburg. It is next to Berlin and part of the larger Berlin/Brandenburg area. Potsdam is by the Havel River, southwest of Berlin's center. Potsdam was the home of Prussian and German kings until 1918. Its design shows ideas from the Enlightenment. It was meant to be a "beautiful, countryside dream" to remind people of their connection to nature and reason. The city has many lakes and famous landmarks, especially the parks and palaces of Sanssouci, the biggest World Heritage site in Germany. The Potsdam Conference in 1945 took place at Cecilienhof Palace. Babelsberg, in the southeast of Potsdam, has been a major film studio since the 1930s. It is still important for film production in Europe. Babelsberg is the oldest large film studio in the world. Potsdam became a science center in the 19th century. Today, there are three colleges, the University of Potsdam, and over 30 research institutes in the city.

Ray Milton Dolby was an American engineer who lived from January 18, 1933, to September 12, 2013. He invented something called Dolby NR, which reduces noise. While working at Ampex, he helped create the video tape recorder. Dolby also started a company called Dolby Laboratories.

Michael Gregory Rowe was born on March 18, 1962. He is an American television host, narrator, and used to be an opera singer. He is famous for hosting "Dirty Jobs" on the Discovery Channel and "Somebody's Got to Do It" on CNN. Currently, he hosts "Returning the Favor" for Facebook, where he finds people doing good things and returns the favor. He also has a podcast called "The Way I Heard It with Mike Rowe," which tells short stories for curious people who have short attention spans. Mike Rowe has narrated shows like "Deadliest Catch," "How the Universe Works," and "Shark Week" on the Discovery Channel, Science Channel, and National Geographic Channel. He has also appeared in commercials for Ford Motor Company. In June 2020, the Discovery Channel announced "Dirty Jobs: Rowe’d Trip," four episodes to be shown in mid-July 2020, described as a mix of a reunion, a road trip, and a look-back-special.

Joe Osborn, born on August 28, 1937, and died on December 14, 2018, was an American bass guitar player. He worked as a session musician in Los Angeles with a group called the Wrecking Crew in the 1960s through the 1980s. He also played with a group of studio musicians in Nashville known as the A-Team during the same period.
Buhler is a city in Reno County, Kansas, United States. In 2010, the city had 1,327 people living there.

Screaming Trees was an American rock band formed in Ellensburg, Washington in 1985. The band members were Mark Lanegan (vocalist), Gary Lee Conner (guitarist), Van Conner (bassist), and Mark Pickerel (drummer). Barrett Martin replaced Pickerel as the drummer later. The band made seven full albums, five EPs, and three compilations. They played a mix of hard rock and psychedelic music. Screaming Trees were known as one of the pioneers of the grunge movement, along with bands like Alice in Chains, Pearl Jam, Nirvana, and Soundgarden. Screaming Trees became famous during the early 1990s grunge era. They had one top ten hit. However, the band faced problems making a follow-up album to "Dust," leading to a long break and their official breakup in 2000.

Hedemora is a town in Dalarna County, Sweden. It had 7,273 people living there in 2010. Despite having a small population, Hedemora is called a "city" for historical reasons. In fact, it is the oldest city in the county. People like Jonas Nilsson, Kerstin Thorborg, Martin Matsbo, Bertil Norman, and Ulf Stenlund are from Hedemora. The town is known for making diesel engines used in ships. For example, these engines are found in submarines built by Kockums, including those in the Royal Australian Navy and the Republic of Singapore Navy. Clifftop Games, an independent game developer based in Hedemora, created games like Kathy Rain and Whispers of a Machine.

The Indian roller, also known as "Coracias benghalensis," is a bird in the roller family. It can be found from west Asia to the Indian subcontinent. The Indian roller is not considered endangered. The Indochinese roller used to be seen as a type of Indian roller. It is famous for flying tricks during breeding season. You often see it sitting on trees or wires near roads. It likes open grassland and scrub forest. India has the most Indian rollers, and some Indian states have chosen it as their state bird.

In 1963, there was a very dangerous hurricane called Flora in the Atlantic. The hurricane season started on June 15 and ended on November 15. That year, there were nine named storms. The first storm, Arlene, hit Bermuda and caused some damage. Other storms like Beulah, Debora, and an unnamed storm did not hit land. In September, Cindy hit Texas and caused some wind damage and flooding. It left three people dead and about $12.5 million in damage. Edith hit the Lesser Antilles and caused 10 deaths and about $43 million in damage, mostly on Martinique. The most serious storm was Flora. It became a very strong Category 4 hurricane. Flora dropped a lot of rain, causing floods that killed at least 7,193 people and caused about $773.4 million in damage. This made Flora one of the deadliest hurricanes on record. Later, in October, Ginny moved off the southeastern United States and hit Nova Scotia, causing at least three deaths and $400,000 in damage. Finally, in November, a tropical storm called Helena hit Guadeloupe, causing five deaths and over $500,000 in damage. Overall, these storms caused at least 7,214 deaths and about $830.1 million in damage.

Vicente Trueba Pérez was born on October 16, 1905, in Sierra Pando, Torrelavega, Cantabria. He died on November 10, 1986. He was a professional road racing cyclist from Spain. He is known for winning the King of the Mountains title in the Tour de France. This means he won the overall classification in the mountains classification of the Tour de France. He also came in sixth place overall in the Tour de France.
Septèmes-les-Vallons is a village in the Bouches-du-Rhône area in southern France. It is about 10. 7 kilometers or 6. 5 miles north of Marseille's center.

In music, a chord progression is a series of chords. It is a key part of the harmony in Western music, from classical music to today. Chord progressions are essential in pop, rock, blues, and jazz music. In these types of music, the melody and rhythm are built around the chord progression. In tonal music, chord progressions help establish or contradict the key of a song. In classical music theory, they are often written using Roman numerals. For example, the progression i–vi–ii–v. In popular and traditional music, chords are often named and described by their quality. For example, in C major, the progression would be C major–A minor–D minor–G major. In rock and blues, musicians also use Roman numerals for chord progressions. For instance, the 12-bar blues often uses the i, iv, and v chords. A simple 12-bar blues might be expressed as i–i–i–i, iv–iv–i–i, v–iv–i–i. Using Roman numerals allows a band leader to instruct a backup band to play in any key. For example, in C major, the chords would be C–C–C–C, F–F–C–C, G–F–C–C. The complexity of chord progressions varies across genres and time periods. Some pop and rock songs from the 1980s to the 2010s use simple progressions. Funk focuses on groove and rhythm, sometimes using just one chord for an entire song. Some jazz-funk songs use a two-, three-, or four-chord vamp. Punk and hardcore punk use a few chords. On the other hand, bebop jazz songs often have more complex progressions, with one or two chord changes per bar.
Lourscheid is a town in the Trier-Saarburg district, which is in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany.

Denisovans are an extinct species or subspecies of ancient human who lived in Asia during the early stone age. They may have survived until around 14,500 years ago in New Guinea. Very little is known about them because only a few remains have been found. Most of what we know comes from DNA evidence. Scientists are still deciding whether to call them "homo denisova," "h. altaiensis," or "h. sapiens denisova." The first Denisovan was identified in 2010 from a young girl's finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia. DNA tests showed they were closely related to Neanderthals. Neanderthals also lived in the cave, but it's not clear if they ever lived there together. Denisovans were found in different habitats, like forests, tundras, mountains, and jungles. Their DNA suggests they had dark skin, eyes, and hair. They were similar to Neanderthals in their build and facial features but had larger molars like some ancient humans and australopithecines. Denisovans interbred with modern humans. About 3-5% of the DNA of some Melanesians and Aboriginal Australians comes from Denisovans, with Papuans having about 6%. There's also evidence they interbred with local Neanderthals, with about 17% of Denisovan DNA from Neanderthals. A hybrid named "Denny" was found with a Denisovan father and a Neanderthal mother. 4% of Denisovan DNA came from an unknown ancient human species that diverged from modern humans over a million years ago.

Questacon, a big science and technology centre, is in Canberra, Australia, by Lake Burley Griffin. It has over 200 fun, interactive exhibits about science and technology. Questacon also runs many programs to encourage Australian children to enjoy and love science.

Peter Neville Luard Pears, born on June 22, 1910, and died on April 3, 1986, was an English singer. He worked closely with composer Benjamin Britten for nearly forty years. At first, Pears was unsure if he should focus on playing or singing. It was not until 1937, when he met Britten, that he decided to become a singer. Britten then wrote many songs and opera roles with Pears in mind. Pears sang in more than ten of Britten's operas. In concerts, Pears and Britten were famous for singing Schubert and Schumann's songs. They recorded most of the works Britten wrote for Pears, as well as music by other composers. Pears performed a wide range of music from different times, from the Tudor period to modern music. He helped found the Aldeburgh Festival in 1947 and the Britten-Pears School in 1972. After Britten's death in 1976, Pears continued to be involved in the festival and the school, where he led the singing department. Pears had a special voice that not everyone liked, but he could sing in many different musical styles.

Edgar Lawrence Doctorow, born on January 6, 1931, and passed away on July 21, 2015, was an American novelist, editor, and professor. He is famous for his historical fiction. People think he was one of the most important American novelists of the 20th century. He wrote twelve novels, three collections of short stories, and a play. His notable works include "Ragtime" (1975), "Billy Bathgate" (1989), and "The March" (2005). These books often had fictional characters in real historical settings, with real historical figures, and used different storytelling styles. Doctorow was praised for his creativity and imagination. Some of his works were made into films, like "Welcome to Hard Times" (1967) with Henry Fonda, "Daniel" (1983) with Timothy Hutton, "Billy Bathgate" (1991) with Dustin Hoffman, and "Wakefield" (2016) with Bryan Cranston. His most famous adaptations were the film and Broadway musical "Ragtime" (1981 and 1998), which won four Tony Awards. Doctorow received several awards, including the National Book Critics Circle Award for "Ragtime," "Billy Bathgate," and "The March," and the American Academy of Arts and Letters Gold Medal for Fiction. Former President Barack Obama called him one of America's greatest novelists.

Roger Mayweather was born on April 24, 1961, in Grand Rapids, Michigan. He was a boxer who fought from 1981 to 1999. Roger was a champion in two different weight classes. He held the WBA and lineal super featherweight titles from 1983 to 1984, and the WBC light welterweight title from 1987 to 1989. He also won the IBO light welterweight title in 1994 and the IBO welterweight title from 1994 to 1995. Roger was the son of Bernice (Ambrose) and Theartha Mayweather. He was part of the Mayweather boxing family, with brothers Floyd Mayweather Sr. and Jeff Mayweather, and nephew Floyd Mayweather Jr. From 2000 to 2012, Roger trained Floyd Mayweather Jr. Under Roger's training, Floyd Jr. became a famous boxer and one of the best in the sport.

Beauty and the Beast: The Enchanted Christmas is a 1997 American movie. It came out directly to video. The movie is about Christmas and is a sequel to the 1991 Disney film Beauty and the Beast. In 1997, it sold 7.6 million VHS tapes. This is the first movie after the original Beauty and the Beast. Another movie, Belle's Magical World, came out in 1998.
Charmes-sur-Rhône is a village in the Ardèche region of southern France.

Aberdeen, pronounced "ablíla" in Lakota, is a city in South Dakota. It is the county seat of Brown County and is located northeast of Pierre. As of the 2010 census, Aberdeen had 26,091 people, making it the third-largest city in the state after Sioux Falls and Rapid City. Aberdeen is part of the Aberdeen micropolitan statistical area, which includes Brown and Edmunds counties and had 40,602 people in 2010. The city is known as a college town because it has Northern State University and Presentation College.
anicadu is a village that is about 4 km from mallapally town. It is in the pathanamthitta district.

Cranbrook is a city in southeastern British Columbia, Canada. It is situated on the west side of the Kootenay River, where it meets the St. Mary's River. Cranbrook is the biggest town in the East Kootenay region. In 2016, the city had 19,259 people, and the larger area had 26,083. Cranbrook is where the Regional District of East Kootenay headquarters are located. It also hosts the regional headquarters of some provincial government offices, including the Rocky Mountain Forest District. The city has a museum about trains called the Canadian Museum of Rail Travel. It shows old passenger train cars from the 1920s and 1900s.

The Swedish Bandy Association is the governing body of bandy in Sweden. It organizes the men's and women's national teams and the men's leagues, Elitserien and Allsvenskan, and the women's league, Damallsvenskan. The association was formed in Stockholm on April 5, 1925, and moved from Katrineholm to Stockholm. Bandy was introduced in Sweden in 1895 by Clarence von Rosen, who learned about the game during a visit to Great Britain. He started the first bandy club in Sweden, Stockholm Hockeyklubb. Bandy was organized within the Swedish Ballgame Association in 1905 and later within the Swedish Football Association. In 1925, 49 clubs came together to form the Swedish Bandy Association. Since 1931, the association organizes national leagues in Sweden. The title of Swedish Bandy Champions is given to the winners of the final match, which is played in March. Before 2013, the association had 23 district associations, but they were replaced by six larger districts for better management: Mellansverige, Nord, Stockholm, Småland, Sydväst, and Västergötland. The Swedish Bandy Association was one of the founding members of the Federation of International Bandy in 1955.
Launay-Villiers is a town in the Mayenne department, located in western France.
Cher is a department in the Centre-Val de Loire region of France. It got its name from the Cher River.

KFUM Örebro is a YMCA association in Örebro, Sweden. It was established in 1890. In 1990, the club won the Swedish women's juniors national volleyball championship. Between 1996 and 2001, the club won the Swedish national women's volleyball championship for six seasons in a row. The men's floorball team played in the Swedish top division during the 1990s.

nuclear weapons testing, uranium mining, and nuclear power have often been discussed in Australia. There has been a long history of anti-nuclear movements in the country. These movements started in the 1970s, when there was debate about French nuclear tests and uranium mining in Australia. Several groups formed to address nuclear issues, including the Movement Against Uranium Mining and Campaign Against Nuclear Energy (CANE), which worked with environmental groups like Friends of the Earth and the Australian Conservation Foundation. In 1983, the new Labor government failed to stop uranium mining, which was a setback for the movement. By the late 1980s, uranium prices dropped, and the costs of nuclear power rose, making the anti-nuclear movement seem successful. CANE was disbanded in 1988. Around 2003, people began to support nuclear power as a way to fight global warming. The Australian government showed interest. However, anti-nuclear campaigners and some scientists argued that nuclear power couldn't replace other energy sources and that uranium mining might produce a lot of greenhouse gases. As of 2015, Australia didn't have any nuclear power plants but had five uranium mines. Four of these were in South Australia, and one was in the Northern Territory. Australia mainly exports the uranium it mines. It doesn't have any nuclear weapons or nuclear-powered ships.

Glasgow Central is one of two main train stations in Glasgow, Scotland. It opened in 1879 by the Caledonian Railway. Network Rail manages it, and it's the northern end of the West Coast Main Line, serving inter-city services between Glasgow and England. The other main station in the city center is unnamed here. In 2017-18, Glasgow Central had nearly 33 million passengers, making it the twelfth-busiest railway station in Britain and the busiest in Scotland. Network Rail says over 38 million people use it yearly, with most being passengers. It's a Category A listed building, meaning it's historically important. In Simon Jenkins' list of "Britain's 100 Best Railway Stations," Glasgow Central was one of ten to receive five stars. In 2017, it got a customer satisfaction score of 95.2%, which was the highest in the UK.

Aerogel is a very light and porous material made by replacing the liquid in a gel with a gas. It's very lightweight and doesn't conduct heat well. People call it "frozen smoke," "solid smoke," "solid air," or "solid cloud" because it's translucent and how light scatters in it. Aerogel feels like soft foam when you touch it. It can be made from different materials. Aerogel was first created in 1931 by Samuel Kistler. He made it by drying a gel without causing it to shrink. Kistler made silica aerogel first, and later worked on alumina, chromia, and tin dioxide aerogels. Carbon aerogels were developed in the late 1980s. The term aerogel is used for materials with a similar structure, not just one specific material.

James Albert Smith Leach, born on October 15, 1942, is an American academic and former politician. He worked as the ninth chair of the National Endowment for the Humanities from 2009 to 2013. Leach was a member of the U.S. House of Representatives for Iowa from 1977 to 2007. He taught at Princeton University as the John L. Weinberg visiting professor of public and international affairs. He also acted as the interim director of the Institute of Politics at the John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University from September 17, 2007, to September 1, 2008. Leach was a Republican in the U.S. House of Representatives for 30 years, from 1977 to 2007. He represented Iowa's 1st district until 2003. In Congress, he was the chair of the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services from 1995 to 2001. He also led the committee's subcommittee on Asian and Pacific Affairs from 2001 to 2006. Additionally, he started and co-chaired the Congressional Humanities Caucus. Leach lost his 2006 re-election to Democrat Dave Loebsack. He is known for sponsoring the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, an important banking law from the 20th century.

edinburgh trams is a tramway in edinburgh, scotland. It is run by edinburgh trams ltd. and runs between york place in the new town and edinburgh airport, with 16 stops. Construction started in june 2008 and opened on 31 may 2014, after facing delays. Initially, the cost was estimated at £375 million in 2003. By 2008, when contracts were signed, the cost had increased to £521 million. After delays, the final cost was £776 million. The scheme became profitable after just two years and surpassed the original ridership goals. In march 2019, edinburgh council approved extending the line from york place to newhaven. The extended line is expected to be operational by early 2023.

Quarten is a municipality in the Sarganserland constituency, in the canton of St. Gallen, Switzerland. It is located above Lake Walensee. The municipality includes Quarten itself, as well as Oberterzen, Unterterzen, Quinten, Mols, Murg, and parts of Tannenbodenalp.

In aesthetics, the uncanny valley is about how people feel when something looks almost like a human but isn't exactly right. It suggests that when objects, like robots or 3D animations, look somewhat human, people might feel strange and uncomfortable. This discomfort creates a "valley" in how much people like the object, as usually, people like more human-like things more. Examples can be found in robots, 3D computer animations, and lifelike dolls. As technology advances and makes these objects look more real, some people might feel a bit eerie or uncomfortable. The uncanny valley idea says that when something seems almost human but isn't quite right, people might feel cold and strange.

André Kirk Agassi, born on April 29, 1970, is an American retired professional tennis player who was once the world's top-ranked player in singles. He won eight Grand Slam titles and a gold medal in the 1996 Olympics. He was also a runner-up in seven other Grand Slam tournaments. Agassi is the first male player to win four Australian Open titles, a record later broken by Novak Djokovic and Roger Federer. He is the second of five male players to achieve the career Grand Slam in the Open Era, and the first to achieve the career Golden Slam (winning all Grand Slams and an Olympic gold medal). He is also the only man to win the ATP Tour World Championships, a distinction known as a "career super slam." Agassi was the first male player to win all four Grand Slam tournaments on three different surfaces (hard, clay, and grass). He won 17 ATP Masters Series titles and was part of winning Davis Cup teams in 1990, 1992, and 1995. He reached world number one in 1995 but faced personal issues in the mid-to-late 1990s, dropping to number 141 in 1997. He returned to number one in 1999 and had his most successful period in the next four years. Agassi, known as "the punisher," retired from professional tennis on September 3, 2006, after losing in the third round of the US Open to Benjamin Becker due to back issues. He founded the Andre Agassi Charitable Foundation, which raised over $60 million for at-risk children in southern Nevada. The foundation also opened the Andre Agassi College Preparatory Academy in Las Vegas, a public charter school for at-risk children. He has been married to fellow tennis player Steffi Graf since 2001.

Lothar Herbert Matthäus, born on March 21, 1961, is a German football manager and former player. He was the captain of West Germany when they won the 1990 FIFA World Cup and lifted the trophy. He was named European Footballer of the Year and was the first to receive the FIFA World Player of the Year award. Matthäus played in five FIFA World Cups (1982, 1986, 1990, 1994, 1998), more than any other outfield player in men's football, until Rafael Márquez tied his record in 2018. He played in 25 World Cup matches, the most by any single player. Matthäus was the captain of the West German team that won the 1990 World Cup in Italy and also led the German squad in the 1994 World Cup in the United States. He also won the UEFA Euro 1980 and played in the 1984, 1988, and 2000 UEFA European Championships. In 1999, at 38 years old, he was again voted German Footballer of the Year, having won it in 1990. Matthäus is the player with the most caps for Germany, retiring with 150 appearances (83 for West Germany) over 20 years and 23 goals. He is part of the FIFA 100 list, chosen by Pelé. Diego Maradona said, "He is the best rival I've ever had. I guess that's enough to define him." Matthäus was known for his passing, sense of position, tackling, and shooting. He usually played as a box-to-box midfielder but later played as a sweeper.
Karl-Josef Rauber, born on April 11, 1934, is a cardinal in the Catholic Church. He worked as a papal nuncio from 1982 until he retired in 2009.

Dwight Lyman Moody, also known as D. L. Moody, was an American preacher who lived from February 5, 1837, to December 22, 1899. He founded the Moody Church, Northfield School (now Northfield Mount Hermon School), and Moody Bible Institute in Massachusetts, and also created Moody Publishers. One of his famous sayings was, "Faith makes all things possible... love makes all things easy." Moody gave up his successful boot and shoe business to focus on spreading his religious message. He worked with the YMCA during the Civil War to help Union troops. In Chicago, he built a major evangelical center that is still operating today. Moody worked with singer Ira Sankey and toured the United States and the British Isles. His speeches were energetic and inspiring, preaching about God's love and kindness, rather than fear and punishment.

Stephanie Murphy was born as Đặng Thị Ngọc Dung on September 16, 1978. She is an American politician from Florida. She belongs to the Democratic Party and represents Florida's 7th congressional district in the United States House of Representatives. She beat the incumbent John Mica in 2016. The district includes parts of Orlando, like downtown and the northern areas, as well as Winter Park, Maitland, Sanford, and Altamonte Springs. Murphy is the first Vietnamese-American woman and the second Vietnamese-American overall to be elected to Congress.

Sir Patrick Head, born on June 5, 1946, co-founded Williams Formula One team. He worked as technical director at Williams Grand Prix Engineering for 27 years. During this time, he made many innovations in Formula One. Sir Patrick was in charge of designing and building Williams cars until May 2004, when his role was taken over by Sam Michael.

Jizya, or jizyah, is a yearly tax historically collected from non-Muslim citizens, known as dhimmis, in Islamic states. Muslim scholars required adult, free, and sane men to pay this tax, while women, children, the elderly, the sick, the mentally ill, monks, hermits, slaves, and musta'mins (non-Muslim foreigners living temporarily) were exempt. Those who joined the military or could not afford to pay were also not required to pay. The Quran and Hadiths mention jizya but do not specify its amount. Early Islamic rulers adapted existing tax systems from conquered lands, such as those from the Byzantine and Sasanian empires. The application of jizya varied throughout Islamic history. Together with kharāj, a term often used interchangeably with jizya, taxes on non-Muslims were a main source of revenue for some Islamic states, like the Ottoman Empire and Indian Muslim sultanates. Jizya rates were usually fixed amounts based on the payer's financial capability. Historically, jizya was seen as a fee for protection, exemption from military service, permission to practice non-Muslim faiths with some autonomy, and proof of submission to Islamic law. Some viewed it as a sign of humiliation for non-Muslims, while others saw it as a source of revenue. Monks and clergy were exempt, leading to debates about its purpose. The term jizya appears in the Quran for a tax from "people of the book," specifically Jews and Christians. Later, followers of other religions, like Zoroastrians and Hindus, were also required to pay jizya. In the Indian subcontinent, the practice ended by the 18th century and almost vanished in the 20th century with the spread of religious tolerance. In modern times, jizya is no longer imposed by nation-states in the Islamic world. However, some organizations, like the Pakistani Taliban and ISIS, have tried to revive it. Some modern Islamic scholars argue that non-Muslims should pay jizya, but moderate Muslims reject the dhimma system, which includes jizya, as inappropriate for modern nation-states and democracies.

Saint-Sauveur-en-Puisaye is a village in the Yonne department, located in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, central France. In the early 1970s, the Château de la Folie, north of the village (between Saint-Sauveur-en-Puisaye and Mézilles), hosted a "Maharishi’s Science of Creative Intelligence" project. People from around the world came to the château to learn transcendental meditation and help renovate the buildings. There were plans to create a meditation campus in the fields between the château and the Etang de la Folie, near the D7 road. However, the project was abandoned in the mid-1970s for unknown reasons.

Rodney Stephen Steiger, born on April 14, 1925, and died on July 9, 2002, was an American actor. He was known for playing unusual, often angry characters. He was called one of Hollywood's most charming and dynamic stars. He was closely connected to method acting, fully becoming the characters he played, which sometimes caused disagreements with directors and co-stars. Steiger played Marlon Brando's mobster brother, Charlie, in "On the Waterfront" (1954), the main character, Sol Nazerman, in "The Pawnbroker" (1964), and the police chief, Bill Gillespie, opposite Sidney Poitier in "In the Heat of the Night" (1967), winning the Academy Award for Best Actor. Born in Westhampton, New York, to a vaudeville performer, his childhood was hard. At 16, he ran away from his alcoholic mother. After serving in the South Pacific during World War II, he started acting on TV in 1947. He got great praise for his role in "Marty" (1953). He made his stage debut in 1946, appearing in "Curse You, Jack Dalton!" and other plays like "An Enemy of the People" (1950), "Night Music" (1951), "Seagulls Over Sorrento" (1952), and "Rashomon" (1959). Steiger first appeared in a film in 1951 in "Teresa." He was in movies like "The Big Knife" (1955), "Oklahoma!" (1955), "Across the Bridge" (1957), and "Al Capone" (1959). His performance in "The Pawnbroker" (1964) led to his role in "Doctor Zhivago" (1965) as an opportunistic Russian politician. In "In the Heat of the Night" (1967), he played a police chief in Mississippi who learns to respect an African-American police officer, Sidney Poitier, and won Best Actor. The next year, he acted as a serial killer in "No Way to Treat a Lady." In the 1970s, Steiger focused on European films, playing Napoleon Bonaparte in "Waterloo" (1970), a Mexican bandit in "Duck, You Sucker!" (1971), Benito Mussolini in "The Last Days of Mussolini" (1975), and a disturbed priest in "The Amityville Horror" (1979). In the 1980s, his health issues, including heart problems and depression, affected his acting career, and he took on smaller roles in low-budget films. His last role was as Judge H. Lee Sarokin in "The Hurricane" (1999), with Norman Jewison, his director from "In the Heat of the Night." Steiger married five times and had a daughter, opera singer Anna Steiger, and a son, Michael Steiger. He passed away on July 9, 2002, in Los Angeles due to pneumonia and kidney failure after gallbladder surgery, survived by his fifth wife, Joan Benedict Steiger.

Suelli, known as Sueddi in Sardinian, is a municipality in the province of South Sardinia, in Italy. It is located near Cagliari. As of December 31, 2004, Suelli had 1,179 people living there and covered an area of. It borders the municipalities of Gesico, Mandas, Selegas, Senorbì, Siurgus, and Donigala.
Remetschwil is a municipality in Baden district, which is in the canton of Aargau, Switzerland.

Suseok, also known as viewing stones or scholar's stones, is a Korean term for small naturally formed or shaped rocks. These stones are traditionally valued, similar to Chinese gongshi and Japanese suiseki. Suseok can be any color and come in different sizes. They can weigh hundreds of kilograms or be much lighter than one kilogram. Suseok are also used in traditional Korean gardens.

Glynis Johns, born on October 5, 1923, is a retired actress from Britain. She acted on stage, TV, and in films, and also danced and played the piano. She was born in Pretoria, South Africa, while her parents were performing there. Johns is famous for playing Desiree Armfeldt in the Broadway show "A Little Night Music." She won a Tony Award for this role. She also played Winifred Banks in the Disney movie "Mary Poppins." In both roles, she sang songs written just for her, like "Send in the Clowns" and "Sister Suffragette." She was nominated for an Oscar for her performance in the 1960 film "The Sundowners." Her voice was known for its deep and smooth quality, and she had a cheerful personality.
Manuele Blasi, born on August 17, 1980, is an Italian former football player who played as a midfielder.

Ketchikan is a city in Alaska, the main town in the Ketchikan Gateway Borough. It's the largest town in Alaska's southeast. Ketchikan's downtown area is a historic district. In 2010, Ketchikan had about 8,050 people, making it the fifth-largest city in Alaska. Including nearby places, the whole borough had about 13,477 people in 2010. The 2017 population estimate was 13,754. Ketchikan became an official city in 1900, making it the oldest city in Alaska. The town is on Revillagigedo Island and gets its name from Ketchikan Creek, which flows through the town. The creek's name might mean "the river belonging to kitschk" or "thundering wings of an eagle."

Teulada (in Latin, "tegula") is a municipality in the province of South Sardinia, which is in the Italian region of Sardinia. It is located southwest of Cagliari. One possible site for the ancient Roman city of Bithia, also called Biotha or Biora, is in the locality of Sant'Isidoro di Teulada. During World War Two, on November 27, 1940, a naval battle took place near Cape Spartivento. HMS Newcastle and three other British cruisers fought against several Italian Navy ships.

Joe Perry, born on September 10, 1950, is a famous American musician and songwriter. He is best known as the lead guitarist and founding member of Aerosmith, a popular American rock band. Aerosmith is often called the "greatest American rock band" and the "bad boys from Boston." They have sold more than 150 million albums worldwide and 70 million in the U.S. alone. Perry also has a solo band called the Joe Perry Project and is part of the All-Star band Hollywood Vampires with Alice Cooper and Johnny Depp. He was ranked 84th in Rolling Stone's list of the 100 greatest guitarists of all time. Perry was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with Aerosmith in 2001. In 2013, he and his songwriting partner Steven Tyler received the ASCAP Founders Award and were inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. In 2014, Simon & Schuster published "Rocks: My Life in and Out of Aerosmith," a book written by Perry with David Ritz.

The Torres Strait is a waterway between Australia and the island of New Guinea. It is about 40 kilometers wide at its narrowest part. To the south is Cape York Peninsula, which is the northernmost part of Australia's mainland. To the north is the Western Province of Papua New Guinea. It was named after navigator Luis Vaz de Torres, who sailed through the strait in 1606.

The first time George Washington became the president of the United States was on Thursday, April 30, 1789. This happened on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City. George Washington started his first four-year job as president that day. Robert Livingston, who was the chancellor of New York, gave him a special promise to be honest in his job. With this, the president's part of the U.S. government began working under the new rules from the 1787 Constitution. John Adams became the first vice president on April 21, 1789, when he started working in the Senate.

Landshut is a town in Bavaria, located in the southeast of Germany. It sits by the river Isar and is the capital of Lower Bavaria, one of seven regions in Bavaria. Landshut is also the main city in the district it governs and has more than 70,000 people. It's the largest city in Lower Bavaria, followed by Passau and Straubing. Landshut is also known as the "City of the Three Helmets" because of its coat of arms. It's famous for the Landshuter Hochzeit, a big medieval festival. Due to its closeness to Munich and the Franz Josef Strauss International Airport, Landshut has become an important place for investments. It's one of the richest industrial towns in Bavaria and has the lowest unemployment rate in East Bavaria.

Leon Jackson, born on December 30, 1988, is a Scottish singer. He won the fourth series of "The X Factor" in 2007. After winning, Jackson starred in an online show called "Leon's Life" from 2007 to 2008. His first album, "Right Now," came out in 2008 and was the 75th best-selling album that year. It included the songs "Don't Call This Love," "Creative," and "Stargazing." Jackson's first single, "When You Believe," sold over 400,000 copies. It was the 92nd best-selling single of the 2000s in the UK and the third best-selling single of 2007. In 2007, Jackson had the best-selling single by a British male artist, beating other popular artists like Mika, Take That, and Mark Ronson. His single "When You Believe" sold more than "Bleeding Love" by Leona Lewis and "Umbrella" by Rihanna. By 2016, Jackson had one UK number one single and two UK top ten singles. His debut album also reached the top five. He spent a total of thirteen weeks in the UK singles charts top 75 with his three charted singles and nine weeks in the UK album charts top 75 with his debut album. "When You Believe" was his winning single from "The X Factor" and is the seventh best-selling single from a "The X Factor" winner. His debut album is the eighth best-selling debut album from a "The X Factor" winner.

Dara Singh Randhawa, born Deedar Singh Randhawa, was an Indian professional wrestler, actor, and politician. He was born on November 19, 1928, and passed away on July 12, 2012. He started acting in 1952. He was the first sportsman to be nominated to India's Rajya Sabha, the upper house. Dara Singh worked as a Hindi and Punjabi film producer, director, and writer. He acted in films and television. He is famous for never losing in wrestling and later becoming a successful movie star. He was well-known for his role as Hanuman in the film "Bajrangbali" (1976) and in Ramanand Sagar's "Ramayan." In 2018, WWE inducted him into the Hall of Fame.

Todor Stoyanov Burmov was born on January 14, 1834, and died on November 7, 1906. He was a key Bulgarian conservative politician and the first prime minister of an independent Bulgaria. Burmov studied at the Kiev Theological Academy and later worked as a teacher in Gabrovo and a newspaper editor. During Ottoman rule, he and Gavril Krastevich were part of a moderate group that wanted an independent Bulgarian Orthodox church linked to the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople. They opposed more extreme nationalists who wanted a complete split. Burmov was close to Alexander of Bulgaria and became the first prime minister of the independent country on July 17, 1879, despite the weak position of the conservatives. His main job was to stabilize the new country, including putting Varna and other areas under martial law because of Muslim uprisings. His government failed due to lack of support from the conservative party in the assembly and fell the same year. After his time as prime minister, Burmov stayed active in politics. He was the finance minister in the governments of Leonid Sobolev and Archbishop Kliment Turnovski. He then returned to journalism and later joined the Progressive Liberal Party led by Dragan Tsankov.

Pinhais is a municipality in Paraná state, Brazil. In 2018, it had 130,789 people. Pinhais became a separate municipality in 1992 from Piraquara. It is part of the Curitiba metropolitan region. Pinhais is the smallest municipality in Paraná by size. It has the Autódromo Internacional de Curitiba and the ExpoTrade Arena within its area.
"Ganbareh" is a song by the German group Sash! It came out on June 24, 2002, through Virgin Records. This was the first single from their fourth album, called "S4! Sash!".

A parody mass is a musical setting of the mass, often from the 16th century, that uses parts of another pre-existing piece of music, such as a motet or a secular song, as its melody. Unlike the other main types of mass compositions from the Renaissance, which use a cantus firmus or a paraphrase, a parody mass takes a polyphonic fragment and uses it in the mass. The term "parody" doesn't mean it's funny; it just refers to using a part of another song. Sacred music like motets were often used, not bawdy secular songs. Some call it an "imitation mass" because "parody" was misunderstood from a 16th-century text. Parody masses were very popular in the Renaissance. Palestrina wrote many of them, and by the 16th century, this style was common. In 1562, the Council of Trent banned using secular music in church, saying nothing profane should be mixed in. They wanted church music to be pure. The rules were mostly followed only in Italy, with some changes already happening in France and ignored in Germany. A parody mass uses a polyphonic fragment, while a paraphrase mass uses only one voice. To make a parody mass, you can add or remove voices, add new material, or use the fragment at the beginning of each part. Pietro Cerone, an Italian music theorist, wrote guidelines for creating parody masses in his 22-volume book. Examples of early parody masses include "Missa malheur me bat," "Missa mater patris," "Missa fortuna desperata" by Josquin des Prez, and "Missa de dringhs" by Antoine Brumel. By the mid-16th century, most composed masses used this technique.

Zifeng Tower, also known as Greenland Center-Zifeng Tower or Greenland Square Zifeng Tower, used to be called Nanjing Greenland Financial Center. It is a very tall building in Nanjing, Jiangsu. Completed in 2010, it has 89 floors. The first 41 floors have shops and offices. Floors 49 to 71 have a hotel, restaurants, and a public viewing area on the 72nd floor. Its design helps separate these sections. Zifeng Tower is the tallest building in Nanjing and Jiangsu. It is the 11th tallest in China and the 20th tallest in the world. The building was designed by the architectural firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, led by Adrian Smith. It covers an area of 18,721 square meters. There is a hotel inside the tower called Nanjing Greenland Intercontinental Hotel.

Jealousy means feeling insecure, scared, and worried about not having enough of something or not being safe. These feelings can come with anger, sadness, feeling not good enough, and feeling helpless. In the past, jealousy meant something different from envy, but now people often use the two words together. Jealousy is common in relationships and has been noticed in babies as young as five months old. Some people think jealousy is a natural feeling in every culture, but others think it depends on the culture. Jealousy can be based on suspicion or reactions. It often happens because of a mix of strong emotions. Psychologists and sociologists study why people feel jealous and how culture affects it. Biologists also look at how our bodies might make us feel jealous without us knowing. Artists and religious leaders have shown their ideas about jealousy through art, films, songs, and teachings.

The Foucault pendulum is a device named after French physicist Léon Foucault. It shows the Earth's rotation. Introduced in 1851, it was the first simple experiment to prove the Earth spins. Today, Foucault pendulums are popular in science museums and universities.

John Singer Sargent, born on January 12, 1856, and died on April 14, 1925, was an American artist living in Europe. He was known as the best portrait painter of his time. Sargent painted about 900 oil paintings and over 2,000 watercolors. He also made many sketches and drawings. Sargent's work showed his travels around the world, including places like Venice, the Tyrol, Corfu, the Middle East, Montana, Maine, and Florida. He was born in Florence to American parents and studied in Paris before moving to London. He lived most of his life in Europe. Sargent became famous as a portrait painter. His first important painting, "Madame X," shown in Paris in the 1880s, was meant to help him become a well-known society painter. Instead, it caused a scandal. After the scandal, Sargent moved to England where he continued his successful career as a portrait artist. Sargent's work showed great skill, especially in his use of a brush. This ability made people admire his work in later years, but it also made some criticize his paintings as too simple. His official portraits were in the grand manner, but his informal paintings showed his connection to impressionism. In his later years, Sargent was not happy with just doing formal portraits. He spent much time on mural painting and painting outdoors. Art historians did not pay much attention to painters who made paintings of royalty and society, like Sargent, until the late 20th century.

The Adult Use of Marijuana Act, or Proposition 64, was a 2016 voter initiative to legalize cannabis in California. Its full name is the Control, Regulate and Tax Adult Use of Marijuana Act. The initiative passed with 57% voter approval. It became law on November 9, 2016, allowing recreational cannabis sales to start in California by January 2018.

David Wayne Parks (December 25, 1941 – August 8, 2019) was an American football player. He played as a wide receiver and end in the NFL. Parks was chosen first in the 1964 NFL draft from Texas Technological College, now known as Texas Tech University. He was picked for three Pro Bowls and was an all-pro selection twice. In 1965, he won the "triple crown" by leading the NFL in receptions, receiving yards, and touchdowns. In 2008, Parks was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame.
